and Food Processing , having been authorized by the Committee to submit the 
Report on their behalf, present this Fifty Fifth  Report on the Demands for Grants 
(2023-2024) of the Ministry of Food Processing Industries,

Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha considered the Demands for Grants (2023-24) of 
the Ministry of Food Processing Industries . The Committee took evidence of the 
representatives of the Ministry of Food Processing Industries at their Sitting held on 
21 February, 2023. The Report was considered and adopted by the Com mittee at 
their Sitting held on 06 March, 2023.

Observations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in Part -II of the 
Report.

information that the y desired in connection wit h the examination of Deman ds for

development of user and environ ment friendly new generation pesticide formulation 
technologies.

INTRODUCTION 
 I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Coal, Mines and Steel having been 
authorised by the Committee to present the Report on their behalf, present this Eleventh 
Report (Eighteenth Lok Sabha) on Action Taken by the Government on the 
Observations/Recommendations contained in the Third Report (Eighteenth Lok Sabha) 
of the Standing Committee on Coal, Mines and Steel on "Demands for Grants (2024-
2025)" relating to the Ministry of Steel.  
2.  The Eleventh Report (Eighteenth Lok Sabha) of the Standing Committee on 
Coal, Mines and Steel was presented to Lok Sabha on 04.12.2024. Replies of the 
Government to all the Observations/ Recommendations contained in the Report were 
received on 18.03.2025. 
3. The Standing Committee on Coal, Mines and Steel considered and adopted 
this Report at their sitting held on 11.08.2025.   
4. An analysis on the Action Taken by the Government on the Observations/ 
Recommendations contained in the Third Report (Eighteenth Lok Sabha) of the 
Committee is given at Annexure-III.

recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in Chapter-I of 
the Report.

As per Section 27 (4) of the Coir Industry Act, 1953 (45 of 1953), every Bye-law made under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is

more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive session aforesaid.
The Section 27 (4) was inserted in the Coir Industry Act based on the Delegated Legislation’s Provisions (Amendment) Act, 1986. Before 1986, it

granted for maintenance of any mode of conveyance. It may be seen that there is no duplication between Regulation 2(28) and Regulation 2(4)

 The  Bank Officer Employee’s (Conduct) Regulations, 
1976, framed under the Banking Companies(Acquisition and 
Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 were examined by the 
Committee and the matter was reported to the House on April 
23, 1999 in the 124 th Report of the Committee.  The 
observations/recommendations of the Committee as contained 
in the said Report are as under:  
 
“5.    The Committee notes with satisfaction that the 
Ministry of Finance as well as the Banks have accepted 
the recommendations of the Committee in relation to 
Regulations 3(1) and 6(4). 
 
6. The Committee notes that the Ministry of Finance 
as well as the Ban ks based in Calcutta and Chennai 
called for no change in relation to Regulation 3(3). The 
Ministry and the Banks had maintained that having 
regard to the nature of work in the banking Industry 
and in the exigencies of work, it was not always possible 
to give written instructions to the subordinates.  It was, 
therefore, submitted by the Banks that no change is 
called for in this regard.  The Committee considered the 
matter and came to the conclusion that any oral 
direction issued under the regulation should always be 
confirmed in writing and there should be no objection 
to this change in the regulation. 
 

7. With regard to Regulation 6(1) the Committee 
observed that while the Indian Bank, Indian Overseas 
Bank and Allahabad Bank maintained that there was 
no need t o specifically mention in the regulation that 
the competent authority must record the reasons for 
directing an official to discontinue honorary work, the 
Chennai based Indian bank had no objection for 
recording in writing of the reasons if so desired

      The Committee examined framing of the subordinate legistation under the Press

finalisation of the rules and regulatons.

absence of regulations duly framed by the Press Council, and approved by 
Government, there was no vacuum in so far as conditions of services of the Council's 
employees were concerned and that until the regulations are so made and notified 
the conditions of service governing the Central Government employees were being 
applied to the Council's employees. The Committee feels that the Press Council has 
a specific and autonomous role to perform and conditions of service of its employees 
have to be drawn up independently in consonance with the nature of its functions.

REPORT 
I 
Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 
  
The Committee examined the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 framed under the 
Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957 and a questionnaire on the subject was 
forwarded to the Ministry of Mines for their comments/ clarifications on the 30th 
October, 2001.  The Committee discussed the matter with the representatives of the 
National Mineral Development Corporation and the Ministry of Mines and the Ministry 
of Steel at Hyderabad on the 8th November 2001. The points referred to theMinistry, 
their comments/ clarifications and the observations of the Committee thereon are 
reproduced below: 
  
I           Point referred  
            Whether the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and amendment thereto have been 
laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha and    if so, the date of laying thereof?   
  
            Ministry’s reply 
            The Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 (MCR, 1960) were laid on the Table of the 
Rajya Sabha on the 6th December 1960, and all amendments thereto have been 
regularly laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha, the last amendment in Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960 dated the 22nd January 2001 was laid in Rajya Sabha on the 2nd 
March 2001. 
  
Committee’s observations 
            The Committee noted that the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and amendments 
thereto were laid on time.  
  
II         Point referred Rule 9 (2) (a): - Application fee 
             
            “A fee calculated in accordance with the provisions of Schedule II.” 
  
               The amount of application fee indicated in Schedule II are nominal. Whether 
Government have any objection in increasing the amount of application to @Rs.500/- 
for first square Km. and Rs.100/- for each additional square Km or any other 
reasonable amounts? 
  
Ministry’s reply 

The Department of Mines may have no objection to an increase in fees payable. 
The Department of Mines has received representations from various State 
Governments also that the application fees are meager and these should be suitably 
enhanced. The matter is already under examination in the Department. However, while 
fixing these rates, it may be kept in view that the fees, by their very nature, are designed 
to cover mainly the processing costs, and, therefore, increasing the existing rates, i.e, to 
Rs 250 for first square kilometer or part thereof, and Rs 50 for each additional square 
kilometer seem justified.

        During the 201 th Session of the Rajya Sabha, 42 Statutory Orders were laid on the 
Table of the House by various Ministries/Departments. The details of the Gazette 
Notifications in which these were publis hed and the date of their laying on the Table of 
the Rajya Sabha have been indicated in the Ministry-wise Statement (Annexure). 
2.     Upon scrutiny of the Orders laid in the Session, the Committee notes that out of 42 
notifications laid, only one notifica tion at Sl. No. 13 laid by the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development, Department of Women and Child Development has been delayed 
by five months and no delay statement has been appended therewith. The Committee 
impresses upon the Ministry of Human Resource  Development (Department of Women 
and Child Development) to pay adequate attention towards the timely laying of the 
subordinate legislation and to append the delay statement in case there is a delay in laying. 
3.     The Committee further notes that three notifications (Sl. No. 3, 7 and 8) laid by the 
Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (Department of 
Telecommunications) bear identical reference number. In this context, the Committee 
would like to invite the Ministry's attention to its fol lowing 
observations/recommendations as contained in the 152nd Report. 
"In the opinion of the Committee, every notification should be assigned a distinctive 
number in order to give it a separate identity and similarly, no notification should 
be published/la id which does not carry a notification number. The Committee 
expects all Ministries/Departments of Government of India to exercise caution in this 
regard. In case where there are more than one notifications under a single file, the 
Ministries/Departments s hould ensure that the file number on each notification 
should be suitably distinguished from one another". 
The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Information Technology (Department of 
Information Technology) would take suitable corrective measures for future.

MODEL FORMULA FOR LAYING OF STATUTORY RULES

BOTH HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT 
        The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha in 
paras 57-58 of its 10th Report presented to the House on the 24th 
May, 1971 had suggested a revised formula for laying of Statutory 
Rules before both Houses of Parliament. Relevant extracts from the 
Report are as under:- 
“Every rule made by the Central Government under this Act 
shall be laid; as soon as may be after it is made, before each 
House of Parliament, while it is in session, for a total period of 
thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or 
more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session 
immediately following the session or the successive sessions 
aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the 
rule or both Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the 
rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be 
of no effect, as the case may be; so, however that any such 
modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the 
validity of anything previously done under that rule. 
        The Committee recommends that the  revised formula 
should be incorporated not only in new legislation but also in the 
existing Acts as and when Bills to amend them are brought 
before Parliament. The Ministry should also incorporate the 
new formula in the Bills pending before Parliament. This will, in 
the opinion of the Committee, bring about uniformity in the 
matter expeditiously.”

member omnibus authority under an Act of Parliament, which may be known as the

sector in the offshore areas, including safety of installations, health safety, and welfare of 
workers and environmental aspects. Relevant extracts from the said report are enclosed

period of six weeks was requested for submission of the ATR. In another communication

December, 1998 as they were engag ed in studying models on which the proposed 
Hydrocarbons Development Authority was to be based, as existing in countries like UK,

The Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 framed under the Securitisation & Reconstruction of Financial Assets &
Enforcement of Security Interest Ordinance, 2002 were examined and a questionnaire was forwarded to the Ministry of Finance (Banking
Division) on the 24 th November, 2003, to which the Ministry replied on the 7 th May, 2004. The Committee considered the Ministry’s
reply at its meeting held on 17 th November, 2005 and decided to seek further clarification on point No.1 (Rule 2 (d) defining ‘Approved
Valuer’). The Ministry vide their communication dated 29th November, 2006 provided the requisite clarification and also gave details of
the changes carried out by the Ministry on the other points on Committee’s suggestion.
 
2.         The points referred to the Ministry, their comments/clarifications and their Action Taken on each point are reproduced below: -
 
1.         Point raised- Rule 2(d) -
“Approved valuer” means a valuer as approved by the Board of Directors or Board of Trustees of the secured creditor, as the case
may be.
Should the approved valuer not be duly qualified; what is the justification for giving full discretion to the secured creditor in this
regard?
 
            Ministry’s comments : (7.5. 2004)
Approved valuer means the professional who is qualified to value the property for a fee.  It is difficult to work out clear-cut
definition making exhaustive list of approved valuers in different fields and types of properties that are to be valued.   It is, however,
suggested that banks and financial institutions may be advised to utilize the services of valuers through Institution of Valuers who
claimed to be the only registered body in the country and their members are bound by code of conduct prescribed by it.  They are covered
by fee prescribed by the Government under Rule 8C of the Wealth Tax Act and also by CBDT.

The Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989. 
 
The Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, framed under the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1988, were examined and a questionnaire was forwarded to the Ministry of 
Shipping, Road Transport and Highways (Department of Road Transport & 
Highway) on the 30th January, 2001 for their comments/clarifications.  The Ministry 
furnished their comments/clarifications on the 3rd April, 2001.  The points referred to 
the Ministry and the comments/ clarifications received thereon are placed at 
Annexure-I.  Comments/suggestions were also invited from a few automobile 
associations on the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 for a comprehensive 
examination of the Rules.  Suggestions were received from the Automobile 
Association of Upper India and the Automobile Association of Southern India which 
were forwarded to the Department of  Road Transport and Highways for 
comments/clarifications on the 20th February, 2002.  The Ministry on the 13th March, 
2002 furnished their comments/clarifications on the issues raised by the Automobiles 
Associations, which are placed at Annexure-II.

the Ministry amended Rules 1(3), 4,5,7,9, 50(1), 75(2) and 89 as per the Committee’s

Report item on 
The Airports Authority of India (Lost Property) Regulations 2003-Implementation 
of 163rd Report of the Committee on Subordinate legislation, Rajya Sabha. 
 
 The Airports Authority of India (Lost Properties) Regulations 2003 framed 
under the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 were examined and the C ommittee 
in its 163rd Report which was presented to the House on 23rd May, 2006 recommended 
as follows:-  
 
 The Committee notes that the Ministry had agreed to replace the words “any 
officer” occurring at a number of places in the Airports Authority of India (Lost 
Property) Regulations, 2003 with the words “Duty Airport manager/Duty Officer 
Control Tower as the case may be”. However, with regard to regulation 6 the 

Committee desired that the Ministry should prescribe a time limit in the regulation 
itself to make it unambiguous and also to ensure that the lost property, if claimed, is 
restored to the rightful claimant within a stipulated time period. The Ministry vide 
their O.M. dated the 21st February, 2006 clarified as under:- 
 
 “Attention of the Committ ee on Subordinate Legislation may be drawn to 
Regulation 7 (1) of the Airports Authority of India (Lost Property) Regulations, 2003, 
wherein a time period of three months for restoring the lost property to the claimant 
has already been prescribed.” 
 
 The Committee thereafter accepted the clarification of the Ministry. 
 
 The Committee notes that the Ministry have agreed to notify amendments in 
regulations 3 (1) and (2) and regulation 4 by substituting the words “any officer” with 
the words “ Duty Airport Manager/Duty Officer Control Tower as the case may be” 
as suggested by the Committee. The Committee hopes that the Ministry shall notify 
the amendment expeditiously.

(ii) 

Report on the 
All India Institute of Medical Sciences Regulations, 1999 
 
 
After the independence of India in 1947, the founding fathers of the country 
visualized the setting up of a world -class institution in the field of medi cal education; 
research and patient care so that the doctors in the country could get the benefit of a 
high standard of medical education and research in the country itself instead of going 
abroad. Accordingly, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences ( AIIMS) was set up as 
an autonomous body under the All India Institute of Medical Sciences Act, 1956. Section 
13 of the AIIMS Act, 1956 outlines the objectives of the Institute as: 
 
a.       to develop patterns of teaching in under -graduate and post -graduate m edical 
education in all its branches so as to demonstrate a high standard of medical education 
to all medical colleges and other allied institutions in India; 
b.   to bring together in one place educational facilities of the highest order for the 
training of personnel in all important branches of health activity; and 
c  to attain self-sufficiency in post-graduate medical education. 
 
2. It was envisaged that there should not be any unwarranted bureaucratic/executive 
control in the day-to-day functioning of AIIMS.  In fact, the then Hon’ble Union Health 
Minister, Madam Raj Kumari Amrit Kaur while piloting the bill with regard to AIIMS 
in Lok Sabha on the 18th February 1956, had specifically stated:  
 
“Subject to such minimum control as the Government of India may ex ercise through its 
rule-making powers, the Institute will enjoy a large measure of autonomy in order that 
it may fulfill the objectives…The Government of India will, of course, make itself 
responsible for providing adequate funds for the maintenance of the institute…. 
The future of the Institute will lie ultimately in the hands of the Directors, the Professors 
and other members of the teaching staff and students…” 
 
3. The AIIMS Act, 1956 provides for framing of rules by the Central Government 
under Section 28 and framing of regulations by the Institute, with the previous approval 
of the Central Government, under Section 29. Accordingly, AIIMS, with the prior 
approval of the Central Government have framed the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences Regulations, 1999.  
 

4. These Regulations were identified for examination by the Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation, Rajya Sabha in 1999 and the Committee had been in correspondence with

THE SENIOR CITIZENS SAVINGS SCHEME, 2004 
  The Senior Citizens Savings Scheme, 2004 framed under the Government 
Savings Banks Act, 1873 was introduced by the Government of India with effect 
from 2nd August, 2004. Citizens of 60 years of age and above as well as citizens 
who have retired on superannuation or otherwise have attained the age of 55 years 
(but less than 60 years) are also eligible to invest their retirement benefits, subject 
to the maximum deposit ceiling provided that the account is opened within one 
month of the retirement. 
2.  The Scheme is operated through a large network of designated post offices 
and branches of public/private sector banks throughout the country. The deposit 
carries interest at the rate of the 9% per annum and interest earned under the 
Scheme is taxable in the hands of the depositor. However, deductions under 
Section 80C of the Income-Tax Act, 1961, is available on deposits up to Rs. 1 
lakh made under the Scheme with effect from 1st April, 2007. 
3.   Due to the importance of the Scheme for the senior citizens, the scheme was 
examined by the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha and a 
questionnaire on the subject was forwarded to the Ministry of Finance 
(Department of Economic Affairs) on the 23rd July, 2008. The Ministry furnished 
their replies on the 29th July, 2008. The points raised by the Committee and the 
comments/clarifications furnished by the Ministry are enumerated in following 
paragraphs. 
4.   The Committee enquired from th e Ministry whethe r any income-tax 
rebate/exemption was admissible under this Scheme. The Ministry replied that 
interest payments under the Scheme had not been exempted from the income tax.

Report on 
The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006  
Originally introduced in 1995, the Banking Ombudsma n Scheme enables speedy and 
cost effective resolution of complaints of bank cus tomers relating to deficiency in 
bank services. The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006 ( Annexure I ) was framed by 
the Reserve Bank of India in exercise of power conf erred by Section 35A of  the 
Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The Scheme was introd uced with the object of 
enabling resolution of complaints relating to certain services rendered by banks and to 
facilitate the satisfaction or settlement of such complaints. The Reserve Bank of India 
is mandated to ensure that all commercial banks, pr ivate banks, regional rural banks, 
and scheduled primary co-operative banks shall comp ly with the Banking 
Ombudsman Scheme, 2006.  The Scheme provides appoin tment of Chief General 
Manager or General Manager of the RBI as Banking  O mbudsmen to be located at 
places identified by the it. Chapter III of the Sch eme defines jurisdiction, powers and 
duties of Banking Ombudsmen. Chapter IV prescribes the procedure for redressal of 
grievances, grounds of complaints, settlement of co mplaints by agreement or award 
by the Banking Ombudsman. The Chapter also gives th e grounds of rejection of 
complaints and appeal against the award given by Ba nking Ombudsman before the 
Appellate Authority.    
1.  The customers can also now complain to the Banking Ombudsman against deficiency 
in almost any banking services (Annexure-II), including credit cards, after 
exhausting the channel available with the bank conc erned for resolving their 
complaints. The Banking Ombudsman tries to resolve the complaint through 
conciliation or mediation and even passes an award if it is not resolved through such 
settlement.   
2.  It was taken up for detailed examination by the Com mittee on Subordinate 
Legislation, Rajya Sabha due to the importance of t he Scheme for general public,. 
Under the Scheme, Ombudsman offices are set up at 1 5 places in different parts of 
country mainly in the State capitals ( Annexure III). Any  person who has grievance 
against a bank on any of the grounds listed in the Scheme can lodge a complaint to 

the Banking Ombudsman (BO) within whose jurisdictio n the branch or the office of 
the bank complained against is located. If the comp lainant is not satisfied with the 
award given by the BO, he can approach the Appellat e Authority for the redressal of 
his grievances.

REPORT ON 
THE BIO-MEDICAL WASTE (MANAGEMENT AND 
HANDLING) RULES, 1998 
  The Bio-Medical Waste (Managem ent and Handling) Rules, 1998 
were framed under Sections 6, 8 and 25 of the Environment (Protection) 
Act, 1986 The Rules were notified on the 20th July 1998 that deal with 
the duties of occupier of the institution generating the bio-medical waste, 
treatment and disposal, segregation,  transportation and storage of bio-
medical waste. The Rules also prescribe the authorities for granting 
authorization and monitoring the implementation of Rules. It also 
prescribe the procedure for reporting and record maintenance. The Rules 
have six Schedules. Schedule I prescribes 10 categories of bio-medical 
waste and procedure of their disposal , Schedule II prescribes color code 
of the container for respective categories of bio-medical waste. Schedule 
III prescribes the label for bio-medi cal waste bags/con tainers. Schedule 
IV prescribes label for transport of such waste, Schedule V provides for 
the standards for the treatment and disposal of bio-medical waste and 
Schedule VI provides that waste treatment facilities like incinerators and 
autoclaves should have been installed,  in all health care facilities by 
December 2002. 
2.   The Rules were examined and a questionnaire on the subject was 
sent to the Ministry of Environment & Forests on January 24, 2000 for 
their comments. The comments/clarifications of the Ministry of 
Environment & Forest on the points raised in the questionnaire were 
received on February 1, 2000 (Annexure-I). 
3.  The Committee found that the Ministry’s replies to most of the 
queries pertained to only couple of Central Government Hospitals located 
in Delhi. The Committee, therefore is constrained to infer that as though 

Rules framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 had all India 
jurisdiction, its implementation has remained very limited. 
4.  The Committee observed that the Rules were silent about the waste 
generated in Pathology labs. It was informed that the waste generated in 
Pathological labs is to be disposed off as per the guidelines for the 
Category I Bio Medical waste. 
5.  The Committee was also informed that steps were being taken to 
create awareness among those running/working in the hospitals, clinics, 
as also the doctors, paramedics an d other stakeholders regarding the 
handling, management and disposal of bio-medical, wastes. The

The Municipal Solid Wastes (Management & Handling) Rules, 2000 
 
Introduction  
The Central Government enacted the Municipal Solid Wastes (Management 
and Handling) Rules, 2000 ( Annexure I)  under Environment Protection Act, 
1986 ( Annexure II) to regulate the management and handling of the municipal 
solid wastes in environmentally acceptable manner. The rules have come into 
force from 25
th September 2000. Salient Features of the Rules are as follows: 
 
●  Municipal solid waste includes commercial and residential wastes generated 
in municipal or notified areas in either  solid or semi-solid from excluding 
industrial hazardous wastes but including treated bio-medical wastes 
● Rules are applicable to every munici pal authority responsible for collection, 
segregation, storage, transportation, pro cessing and disposal of municipal solid 
wastes. 
● Every municipal authority within the te rritorial area of the municipality is 
responsible for the implementation of th e provisions of these rules and for any 
infrastructure development for collection, storage, se gregation, transportation, 
processing and disposal of municipal solid wastes. 
● Local bodies were required to set up waste processing and disposal facilities 
before 31.12.2003. 
 
Guidelines/norms to be followed for handling municipal solid wastes have been 
provided in the Schedules and these relate to; 
 
• Prohibition of littering of solid wastes 
• Organizing house to house collection of waste 

 6
• Proper collection of waste from slums and squatters, hotels, restaurants, 
office complexes and commercial areas 
• Waste not be burnt 
• Organising awareness programmes for segregation of wastes  
•  Proper maintenance of waste storage facilities 
• Covering of vehicles used for transportation of wastes 
• Adopting suitable waste processing technol ogies to make use of wastes so 
as to minimize burden on landfill. 
•  Restricting land filling for non-biodegradable inert waste 
•  land filling operations to  follow prescribed proce dure to prevent pollution 
problem

 1.2     The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the

Emblem of India (Regulation of Use)  Rules, 2007 and the Public Liability 
Insurance Rules, 1991 and issues relating to them  along with the comments 
received from the Government.  The observations and recommendations of the

The Public Liability Insurance Rules, 1991 
 
 The Central Government framed the P ublic Liability Insurance Rules, 1991 
(Annexure I)  under the  Public Liabi lity Insurance Act, 1991  (Annexure II) 
which is the first of its kind as it provides for an insurance policy to give an 
immediate relief to general public on th e principle of ‘NO FAULT LIABILITY’. 
With this objective, the Rules establis h a regime of prevention and providing 
immediate relief to the victims resulting fr om activities related to the handling of 
hazardous substances and makes owners legally liable for compensating any 
damage caused by them. Under  the rules,  the owner is required to assess the 
hazards of the installation take all preventi ve measures to minimize the risk and to 
reduce the extent of damage. The owners as well as authorities are required to be in 
total preparedness to fight any emergency at their installations.The Rules came into 
force on 15
th May, 1991. 
 
2. The first set of Rules, 'The Public  Liability Insurance Rules, 1991' have 
since gone through three amendments. The fi rst amendment to the Rules called the 
 Public Liability In surance (Amendment) Rules, 1991 was published & 
came into force on 20
th September, 1991 (Annexure III). The second amendment 
to these Rules  known as the Public Liability Insurance (Amendment) Rules, 1992 
came into force on 6
th February, 1992 (Annexure IV). The third amendment of 
these Rules known the Public Liability Insurance (Amendment) Rules, 1993 came 
into force on 23rd April, 1993 (Annexure V). 
3. The following aspects have been elaborated in the rules:- 
i) Procedure for claims for relief 
ii) Powers of the Collector 
iii) Application form for compensation 
iv) Procedure and manner of giving directions 
v) Form of  Notice 

vi) Extent of Liability of the Insurance 
 
 
The General Insurance Corporation (GIC ) is the insurer under the Act and 
has floated policies to this effect. It is  the responsibility of  the GIC to collect 
premium and money for the ERF. 
 
4. The Public Liability (Insurance) Rules, 1991 were examined and a 
questionnaire was forwarded to the Ministry of Environment & Forests on 12
th 
May, 1999 for furnishing their comments thereon. The comments received from the 
Ministry of Environment & Forests (Annexure VI)  were considered and taken up 
by the Committee subsequently.

(I)  
The Railways (Punitive charges for overloading of wagon) Rules, 2007 
 
 
 The Railways (Punitive c harges for overloading of wagon ) Rules, 
2007 (Annexure-I) framed under the Railways Act, 1989 (Annexure-II) were 
notified on 15.06.2007. 
  
2. The main objective  to notify these rules was  to check overloading  of 
wagons and to ensure safe train operation as overloading of wagons 
endangers  the safety of the wagon and track.  As loading in railway wagons 
cannot b e precisely controlled, provision of loading tolerance have been 
made in the rules.  Besides, these rules also intend to check revenue leakage 
caused by understating of weight of consignment loaded in railway wagons. 
To overcome the menace of overloading rules of punitive charges have been 
made stringent for those rail users who have malafide intention. 
The operational benefit of these rules is that it ensure safe train operation 
and prevent leakage of revenue. 
 
3.  The Ministry has informed in th eir background note (Annerxure- III) 
that the incidence of overloading, in case of  West Central and East Central 
for a particular month of 2008 in comparison to corresponding mont h of 
2007 has decreased due to levy of punitive charges for overloading. The 
incidence of overloaded wagons in West Central Railway has reduced to 
10.6% from 22.08% whereas in East Central Railway it has reduced to 
4.76% from 11.28% 
 

4.  The Railway s (Punitive charges for overloading of wagon)  Rules, 
2007 framed under the Railway s  Act, 198 9 were examined and a 
questionnaire on the subject was forwarded to the Ministry of Railways for 
their comments/clarifications on 16 th May, 2008.  The Ministry furnished 
their comments/clarifications on 16th June, 2008 (Annexure IV). 
 
5.  On the query that  what changes took place at the ground level that 
necessitated the supersession of the Rules of 2005 and what are the salient 
features of the new set of rules’ and what loop -holes in the previsous rules 
have been plugged through the new rules?  The Ministry replied that: 
“After the issue of Railways (Punitive charges for overloading of wagon ) 
Rules, 2006 following changes took place: 
 The concept of charging of freight on the basis of CC commodities 
and Enhanced CC commodities was done way with w.e.f 01.03.0 7.  
The freight was chargeable on the basis of permissible carrying of the 
wagons. 
 Loading tolerance  of 1 tonne was provided for all covered wagons 
and BOY/ BOYN tolerance of wagons and loading tolerance of 2 
tonnes was provided for all other wagons (except  covered and 
BOY/BOYN wagons) 
 The above changes necessitated for the amendments in the Railways 
(Punitive charges for overloading of Wagons) Rules, 2006.  Therefore, in 
supersession of Rules of 2006, Railways (Punitive charges for overloading 
of Wagons) Rules, 2007 were notified on 15.6.2007. 
Salient features of Railways (Punitive charges for overloading of Wagons) 
Rules, 2007 are as under: 

 Punitive charges are levied wagon-wise for all commodities instead of 
‘CC’ & ‘Enchanced CC’ comm odities wise as was e arlier in Rules of 
2006. 
 Loading tolerance of 2 tonnes have been provided for all type of 
commodities.  BOY, BOYN, covered, Tank wagons and container 
trains are exceptions in which loading tolerance is one tonne. 
 Graded punitive charges, as prevalent earlier have been retained. 
 There was no loop -holes in the  previous Rules of 2006.  But as the 
system of charging of freight had undergone a change, the rules for punitive 
charges for overloading accordingly needed a corresponding change which 
has been done with the issue of Rules of 2007”. 
 
6.  The Committee wanted to know that the rationale behind levying 
punitive charges three times of the freight rate applicable to the highest class 
in case of overloading by more than five tonnes while provision already 
exists of levying two times of the freight rate in case of overloaded by more 
than two tones for eight wheeled wagons ( except BOX and BOST wagons)

Report on the  
Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and 
Conditions of Service) Central Rules, 1998  
 
  
 The building and other construction workers are on e of the most vulnerable 
segments of the unorganized sector workers in India. Their work is of a temporary nature.  
Besides, relationship between employer and employee  is also temporary and the working 
hours very uncertain. Basic amenities and welfare f acilities provided to these workers are 
found to be generally inadequate. Nature of work in volved in building and construction 
activities is generally arduous and workmen engaged  therein are prone to frequent 
accidents sometimes leading to death due to absence  of adequate safety measures 
available.  
 
2. Down-sizing and outsourcing have also had a nega tive impact on management of 
health and safety of the workers in construction industry. Informal contractual conditions, 
fear of losing employment makes it further difficul t for construction workers to exercise 
their rights.  Often, time and financial constrains  compel employers to ignore the health 
and safety of workers even if that results in their death. 
 
3. Keeping in view the above circumstances the Buil ding and other Construction 
Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of  Service) Act, 1996 was enacted 
by the Parliament to regulate the employment and co nditions of service of building and 
other construction workers and to provide for their  safety and welfare measures. The  
Building and other Construction Workers (Regulation  of Employment and Conditions of 
Service) Rules, 1998 ( Annexure I ) framed under the above Act were taken up for 
examination by the Committee keeping in view its importance in July, 1999. 
 
4. The Committee discussed the subject with the rep resentatives of the National 
Building Construction Corporation Ltd. (NBCC) and t he Ministries of Urban 
Development and Labour and Employment on 22 
nd  October, 1999 at New Delhi for 
eliciting requisite inputs on the subject matter. D uring the course of the discussion, the 
Committee was apprised of the fact that even though  the construction workers were 
covered to some extent by various labour laws, but being a special category of workers it

Report on the Haj Committee Rules, 2002. 
 
 The Ministry of External Affairs framed the Haj Com mittee Rules, 2002 
(Annexure-I) in exercise of powers conferred by Section 44 of the Haj Committee Act, 
2002.  The Rules prescribe the manner of nomination  or election of the Members of the 
Committee; convening of meetings of the Committee; powers and duties of Chairperson; 
allowances and other terms and conditions of Chairp erson, Vice-chairpersons and 
Members; functions, powers and duties of the chief executive officer; provision for the 
custody of the Central Haj Fund; application of Cen tral Haj Fund; entering into contracts 
and incurring of expenditure by the Committee; prep aration, submission and approval of 
the budget of the Committee; maintenance of account s, auditing and publication; returns, 
statements and reports to be submitted by the Commi ttee; and, control of the Committee 
in respect of financial matters. 
 
2. The rules were examined by the Committee on Subo rdinate Legislation, Rajya 
Sabha and a questionnaire on the subject was forwar ded to the Ministry of External 
Affairs on the 24 
th  September, 2003.  The Ministry furnished their 
comments/clarifications on the 5 th  July, 2005. ( Annexure- II).  The points referred to the 
Ministry and their comments/ clarifications thereon  are reproduced in the subsequent 
paragraphs. 
 
3. Rule 7(2) authorizes the Chairperson to disallow  a proposal moved by any 
member, where the member or his partner or any othe r associate is directly or indirectly 
interested in the management or direction of any bu siness relating to the pilgrims traffic 
or in which any one of them is professionally inter ested on behalf of a person engaged in 
such business.  In this regard, the Committee sugge sted that there should be provisions in 
the rule rendering it obligatory on the part of the  members to disclose any interest in the 
management of any business relating to pilgrims tra ffic, etc.   The Ministry responded 
that it would be a good idea to ascertain such info rmation through individual declaration 
at the time of their selection/nomination to the Co mmittee and the possibility of dealing 
with it will be explored in consultation with the Legislative Department of the Ministry of 
Law & Justice.

Report on the Tuticorin Port Trust Employees (Recruitment, Seniority and 
Promotion) Regulations, 2008  
 
The Tuticorin Port Trust Employees (Recruitment, Se niority and Promotion) 
Regulations, 2008 (Annexure-I)  were framed in exercise of powers conferred by Sec tion 
28 of the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963. The Regulati ons superseded the Tuticorin Port 
Trust Employees (Recruitment, Seniority and Promoti on) Regulations, 1979 and 
prescribe the manner of appointment/recruitment, fi xation of seniority and promotion of 
employees of Tuticorin Port.  
 
2. The Regulations were taken up for examination by  the Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation, Rajya Sabha and a questionnaire on the  subject was forwarded to the 
Ministry of Shipping for their comments/clarificati ons on the 9 
th  March, 2010. The 
Ministry furnished their comments/clarifications on  the 7 th  June, 2010 (Annexure-II) . 
The important points/issues raised by the Committee  and the comments/clarifications 
furnished by the Ministry are elaborated in the succeeding paragraphs.

Seniority and Promotion) Regulations, 2008 have bee n framed in supersession of the 
Tuticorin Port Trust Employees (Recruitment, Senior ity and Promotion) Regulations, 
1979.  On the reasons that necessitated the framing  of new/revised Tuticorin Port Trust 
Employees (Recruitment, Seniority and Promotion) Re gulations, 2008, the Ministry in 
their written reply submitted that the Ministry of Shipping on the 16 
th  October, 1996 had

Secretary to the Government of India to recommend o n pay and allowances of Class I

report regarding revision of pay and allowances of Class I & II officers in the Major Port

collecting evidence.

THE TEA (DISTRIBUTION AND EXPORT) CONTROL ORDER, 2005 
 
 The Tea (Distribution and Export) Control Order, 2 005 ( Annexure I ) has been 
framed under the Tea Act, 1953 ( Annexure II ). This Order has been framed superseding 
the Tea (Distribution and Export) Control Order, 19 57, and seeks to ensure that all tea 
consignments meant for imports or exports would hav e to undergo a certification 
procedure under which the quality of tea and the co untry of its origin would be 
determined and displayed. The Tea Board has been de signated the nodal agency for this 
certification exercise. Further, the non-preferenti al certification of origin of each 
consignment of tea exports would be issued by the T ea Board or any of its designated 
agencies. The basic objective of this Order is to retain the brand equity of Indian tea.  
 
2. The Committee took up for examination of the sai d Rules and a questionnaire was 
forwarded to the  Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce & Industry on 22 
nd

The points raised by the Committee and the comments  of the Ministry are reproduced 
below:

 The Committee wanted to know about the reasons for  framing the Tea 
(Distribution and Export) Control Order, 2005 which  has been framed in supersession of 
the Tea (Distribution and Export) Control Order, 19 57, the major points of distinction 
between the Orders of 1957 and 2005, and the salient feature of the new Order? 
In response the Ministry informed the Committee tha t the new control order were 
framed in supersession of the earlier Tea (Distribu tion and Export) Control Order, 1957 
for strengthening the surveillance work of the Tea Board, to ensure standard of quality of 
tea for export/import and to maintain image of Indi an tea in the overseas market. The 
main reasons  to frame the Order and objectives thereof are as follows:

The Regional Rural Banks (Appointment and Promotion of
Officers and Employees) Rules, 2010
The Regional Rural Banks were initially established under the provisions
of the Ordinance promulgated way back on 26th September, 1975 and
thereafter under the provisions of the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 with a
view to develop the rural economy and to create an alternative channel to the
‘cooperative credit structure’. The RRBs are jointly owned by the Government
of India, the concerned State Government and Sponsor Banks with issued
capital which is shared by them in proportion of 50%, 15% and 35%
respectively. The area of operations of RRBs is as specified in the notification
issued by the Central Government in a State or a Union Territory.
2. In 2007, a Committee was set up under the Chairmanship of Dr. Y .S.P.
Thorat, the then Chairman of NABARD to examine the manpower norms in
RRBs and to have a standard method of manpower assessment and planning.
The said Committee examined the related issues which had a bearing on
development of appropriate human resources in RRBs vis-à-vis the Model
RRB Officers and Employees Service Regulations, 2000 and RRBs
(Appointment and Promotion of Officers and other Employees) Rules, 1998.
The Committee inter-alia recommended that there was need to revisit the
Model RRB Officers and Employees Service Regulations, 2000 in the changed
scenario especially, after the restructuring of RRBs by way of amalgamation.
In view of that, a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri Amresh Kumar,
Executive Director, NABARD was constituted for a comprehensive review of
the RRB (Appointment and Promotion of Officers and other Employees) Rules,
1998. This Committee submitted its report in February, 2009 and after
consultations with NABARD and Ministry of Law and Justice the revised
Regional Rural Banks (Appointment and Promotion of Officers and Employees)
Rules, 2010 were notified on 13th July, 2010 ( Annexure I).

Report on the Gas Cylinder Rules, 2004  
 
The Gas Cylinder Rules, 2004 (Annexure-I)  were framed in exercise of powers 
conferred by Sections 5 and 7 of the Explosives Act , 1884. These Rules were framed in 
supersession of the Gas Cylinder Rules, 1981 for en suring safety in possession, filling, 
transportation and use of industrial gases. The eig hties and nineties witnessed massive 
expansion in the gas and related industries trigger ed by economic liberalization and 
globalization, use of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) , introduction of Compressed 
Natural Gas (CNG) and entry of new technologies nec essitated the framing of new Gas 
Cylinder Rules, 2004. 
 
2. The scope of the Gas Cylinder Rules, 2004 was wi dened to cover the application 
of the gas cylinder as automotive fuel storage tank s, cylinders made of materials other 
than metals paving way for entry of latest technolo gy in the field of cylinder 
manufacturing, CNG fueling stations and cylinders e xceeding water capacity of 1000 
litres for specific industrial applications. 
 
3. The Gas Cylinder Rules, 2004 outline provisions with regard to filling, 
possession, import and transport of cylinders; valv e specifications for different types of 
cylinders viz. industrial gas cylinders, medical ga s cylinders, domestic and other 
cylinders; safety relief devices; marking on cylind ers; marking on valves; identification 
of colours; labeling of cylinders; restriction on delivery or dispatch of cylinders; repairing 
of seamless gas cylinders during use; repairing of welded or brazed cylinders; prohibition 
of employment of children and intoxicated persons; prohibition of smoking, fires, lights 
and dangerous substances; general precautions, etc. The Rules also provide guidelines for 
examination and testing of cylinders.  
 
4. The Rules were taken up for examination by the C ommittee on Subordinate 
Legislation, Rajya Sabha and a questionnaire on the  subject was forwarded to the 
Ministry of Commerce & Industry (Department of Indu strial Policy & Promotion) for

The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), an autonomous statutory
organization, came into existence after repealing of erstwhile Indian Standards
Institution (Certification Marks) Act, 1952, through an Act of Parliament i.e.
the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 dated 26th November 1986, on
1 April 1987. The new Act has, therefore, a broadened scope with more powers
taking over the staff, assets, liabilities and functions of erstwhile Indian
Standards Institution (ISI). Through this change over, Government envisaged
building a climate for quality culture and consciousness and greater participation
of consumers in formulation and implementation of national standards.

The Border Roads Engineering Services Group ‘A’ (Amendment) Rules, 1988  
 
 Government of India set up the Border Roads Develo pment Board (BRDB) on 14 th  
March, 1960 to expedite road construction work in N orth East and States bordering 
neighbouring countries for socio economic developme nt of remote and far flung areas and to 
provide better road connectivity along the borders.  To execute the road projects approved by 
Government of India and included in BRDB programme,  a self sufficient departmental road 
construction work force in the name of General Rese rve Engineering Force (GREF) popularly 
known as Border Roads Organisation (BRO) was raised on 16 th  June, 1960.  
2. The Border Roads Development Board transacts its  business according to the Rules of 
Business made by the Chairman, BRDB. According to t he BRDB Rules of Business, the Board 
exercises financial and administrative powers of th e Department of Government of India, 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways. The Financia l Advisor (Defence, Finance) is also 
financial advisor to the Board. 
3. Secretary, BRDB is an Ex officio  Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Minist ry of 
Road Transport & Highways and the Secretariat of BR DB is a department of the Ministry of 
Road Transport & Highways which is the administrati ve Ministry of GREF/BRO employees. 
GREF/BRO was made permanent department of the Centr al Government in 1969 and its 
employees were declared Central Government Civilian  employees. The service terms and 
conditions of the GREF employees are governed under  the CCA (CCS) Rules, 1965 and for 
limited purpose of discipline GREF employees are also subject to certain provisions of the Army 
Act, 1950 under Section 4(1) and 4(4) under Article  33 of the Constitution of India so that they 
can discharge their duty within strict discipline.   The fundamental right of GREF employees 
such as to form association, demonstration and stri ke against exploitation in service and 
interaction with press stand restricted as they are restricted for the Defence and Armed Forces of 
India such as Navy, Air Force, Army, CRPF ITBP, Assam Riffle, BSF etc.  
4. The Rules under examination i.e. the Border Road s Engineering Services Group ‘A’ 
(Amendment) Rules, 1988 (Annexure I ) were issued as an amendment to Schedule under  Ru le 
6 (i) of the BRES Service Rules 1977 published unde r G. S R 1554 dated 20 
th  September 1977.

INTRODUCTION 
 
1. I, the Chairperson of the Committee on Subordina te Legislation, having been authorized by the 
Committee, do hereby present on its behalf, this Two Hundred and Twelfth Report of the Committee.  
2.  The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya  Sabha is constituted under Rule 204 of the Rules 
of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council  of States.  Mandate of the Committee is to scrutin ize 
and report to the Council whether the powers to make rules, regulations, bye-laws, schemes or other statutory 
instruments conferred by the Constitution or delega ted by Parliament have been properly exercised with in 
such conferment or delegation as the case may be.  The Notifications containing Rules/Regulations, etc . 
which are laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha are perused by the Committee in the light of the provisions of 
the Acts under which these were framed and also wit h a view to see whether these have been laid proper ly 
and within the prescribed form and time-frame.   
3. The Committee's concern is centered mainly aroun d the serious implications of delayed framing and 
laying of notification containing rules/regulations /orders, etc.  As part of this exercise, Committee has been 
calling the defaulting Ministries/ Departments to k now the reason for the delay, the problems faced by  them 
in laying the notifications and to find solutions to the problems.  
4. The Report has been dealt with in four parts.  T he first part deals with delay in the framing of ru les/ 
regulations under the various Acts of Parliament.  The second part deals with delay in the laying of

I BACKGROUND 
 
 
 Marble a ‘minor mineral’ as defined in clause (e) of Section 3 of Mines and 
Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 is used widely in buildings, monuments 
and sculptures. It is know for its pleasant colours , smooth and uniform texture, moderate 
hardness, amenability to be quarried into big block s, smooth & shiny polished surface 
and silky feel. Though the occurrence of Marble has  been reported from many States in 
the country, however, deposits of economic importan ce are localized in Rajasthan, 
Gujarat, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh and also in Madhya  Pradesh as per recent reports. 
Rajasthan has the distinction of having the best am ong Indian resources of good quality 
marble. As per available data on marble resources a bout 64% of total resources are in 
Rajasthan and 21% in Jammu & Kashmir. The remaining  resources are distributed 
mainly in Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Harya na, Uttarakhand and Sikkim in 
descending order. In terms of production Rajasthan alone accounts for 94% of the total 
output. Further, over the years the export of marble has also increased.  
 
2. The Marble Development & Conservation Rules (MDM R), 2002 were brought 
into effect for the purpose of conservation, system atic development and scientific mining 
of marble and to provide a uniform framework that w ould be applicable throughout the 
country. In the background to these Rules it was in formed that a Group on Marble 
Development (GMD) was constituted on 22.9.1999 unde r the overall guidance and 
supervision of Granite Development Council to addre ss the difficulties faced by the 
Marble industries.  The Group on Marble Development  (GMD) in its meeting held on 2 
nd  
February, 2000 decided to constitute a Sub-Group un der the Chairmanship of Controller 
General, Indian Bureau of Mines to examine the mech anization in marble quarries. The 
Sub-Committee recommended that Marble Development a nd Conservation Rules could 
be framed in line with the Granite Conservation and  Development Rule, 1999.   
Accordingly, in consultation with stakeholders, the  Marble Development and 
Conservation Rules ( Annexure-I) were notified vide G.S.R. 369 (E) dated 15.5.2002.

REPORT 
 
 
Report on the taking over of  Distance Education Council (DEC) of IGNOU by the 
University Grants Commission (UGC) through an administrative order in violation 
of IGNOU Act, 1985 and the Statutes framed thereunder  
 
The Distance Education Council (DEC), which had bee n created and was 
functioning under Indira Gandhi National Open Unive rsity (IGNOU), Act 1985 was 
abolished and its mandate was given to the Universi ty Grants Commission (UGC) and 
All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE) through an administrative order of the 
Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD) dated  29 December 2012 
(Annexure-I). This was  done  without making the necessary amendments in the IGNO U 
Act, 1985 which mandates IGNOU inter alia  to regulate distance education in the 
country.   DEC, which regulated distance education in the country, had come into 
existence as an authority of IGNOU under Statute 28   framed in exercise of powers 
conferred by Section 16 of the IGNOU Act, 1985.  No w, transferring the mandate given 
to IGNOU (read DEC) to the UGC & AICTE raises the following questions:  
(i)  whether an administrative order can undo something that was created 
under a law passed by Parliament;  
(ii)  whether this can be done without amending the IGNOU Act;  
(iii)  whether UGC and AICTE Acts provided for regulating the Open & 
Distance Learning (ODL) mode of education;  
(iv)   whether the Ministry was legally right in taking such a decision; and  
(v)  whether Ministry of Law was consulted before taking such a recourse?

DRAFT REPORT  
ON  
THE KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES COMMISSION RULES, 2006  
  
I.  BACKGROUND 
 
The Khadi and Village Industries Commission Rules, 2006 (Annexure-I)  
were framed in supersession of the Khadi and Villag e Industries Commission 
Rules, 1957, in exercise of powers conferred by Sec tion 26 (1) and (2) of the 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956. The rules were taken up for 
detailed examination by the Committee and a questio nnaire on the subject was 
forwarded to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Mediu m Enterprises for their 
comments/clarifications on 22 nd  August, 2007. The Ministry furnished their 
replies on 8 th  February, 2008 (Annexure-II) . During the course of its 
examination, the Committee also had discussion with  the representatives of (i) 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Sta te Government of Jammu 
& Kashmir along with the Ministry of Micro, Small &  Medium Enterprises at 
Srinagar on 30 th  June 2012 and (ii) KVIC, State Government of Mahar ashtra 
along with the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium En terprises at Mumbai on 
11 th  November 2014. Study note on the said study visits  are enclosed as 
Annexure-III & Annexure-IV respectively.  
 
2. The Committee enquired about the reasons that ne cessitated the framing of 
the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Rules, 2006, in supersession of the 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission Rules, 1957 . The Ministry replied that  
with a view to revamp the structure and functioning  of KVIC, the Government 
had constituted an Expert Committee in December 200 4 to recommend suitable 
measures for revamping of KVIC after reviewing its structure, functioning and 
performance. Based on the recommendations of the Ex pert Committee, KVIC 
(Amendment) Bill, 2005 to amend the KVIC Act, 1956 was drafted and 
introduced in the Lok Sabha on 22 
nd  August, 2005 and finally the KVIC 
(Amendment) Bill, 2005 as passed by both Houses of Parliament, after receiving 

the assent of the President in March 2006, became a n Act of Parliament and the 
amended provisions came into force with effect from 15 th  May, 2006.

Introduction 
 
1.  The National Trust for Welfare of Persons with Auti sm, Cerebral Palsy, Mental 
Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act, 1999 (Commonly known as National Trust Act, 1999) 
was enacted on 30 
th  December, 1999. The Sections 34 & 35 of this Act p rovide for framing 
Rules and Regulations by the concerned Ministry as subordinate legislation.  As per its mandate, 
the Committee amongst others, scrutinizes the rules /regulations so made and reports to the 
Parliament its findings.  The Committee found that following rules and regulations have been 
prepared.   
 
(i)  National Trust for Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental 
Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Rules, 2000 (notified on 26 th  July, 2000; and  
 
(ii)  National Trust Regulations, 2001 (notified on  3 rd  August, 2001).  
 
Mandate of the Act  
 
(ii)  The Act is a progressive piece of legislation which  seeks to achieve the following 
objectives: 
 
1.  to enable and empower Persons with Disabilities (Pw Ds) to live as independently 
and as fully as possible within and as close to the community to which they belong; 
2.  to strengthen facilities to provide support to PwDs to live within their own families; 
3.  to extend support to registered organizations to pr ovide need based services during 
period of crisis in the family of PwDs; 
4.  to deal with problems of PwDs who do not have family support; 
5.  to promote measures for the care and protection of PwDs in the event of death of 
their parent or guardian; 

6

requiring such protection; 
7.  to facilitate the realization of equal opportunitie s, protection of rights and full 
participation of PwDs; and  
8.  to do any other act which is incidental to the aforesaid objects.

Report 
On  
The Reverse Mortgage Scheme, 2008  
 
The Reverse Mortgage Scheme, 2008 ( Annexure I ) has been framed by the Central Board 
of Direct Taxes with an intent to monetize the hous e of a Senior Citizen  as an asset and the 
owners equity in the house. The Scheme involves the  senior citizen as borrower mortgaging the 
house property to a lender, who then makes periodic  payments to the borrower during the latter’s 
lifetime.  The Senior citizen borrower is not requi red to service the loan during his life time and, 
therefore, does not make monthly repayments of prin cipal and interest to the lender. On the 
borrower’s death or on the borrower leaving the hou se property permanently, the loan is repaid 
along with accumulated interest, through sale of the house property.  
2. The proportion of Senior Citizens as well as the ir dependency in the old age is increasing 
in the country. While on the one hand, there is sig nificant increase in longevity, on the other hand, 
cost of good health care facilities is also spirali ng and there is little social security. Senior citi zens, 
therefore, need regular cash flow for supplementing  their pension or other income scheme to 
address their financial needs.  
3. Keeping these issues in consideration and also t he fact that for most senior citizens, the 
house is the largest component of their wealth, the Committee took up for detailed examination the 
Reverse Mortgage Scheme, 2008. A questionnaire on t he Scheme was forwarded to the Ministry 
for their comments/ clarifications which have since  been received ( Annexure II ). The Committee 
also took up for discussion the said Scheme in its meetings held at Mumbai, Udhagamandalam and 
Bangalore on 24 
th  May,  2010; 28th  May, 2010; and, 30 th  May,  2010, respectively.  Study Notes on 
the said discussions are enclosed ( Annexure III, IV and V ). The Committee also had detailed 
discussion with the State Bank of Travancore at Kum aracom on 22 nd  June, 2011 and with IDBI 
Bank at Mumbai on 27 th  September, 2011.  Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Studies) 
was also present on both the meetings.  Study Note on the said discussions are enclosed 
(Annexure VI and VII respectively).  The points raised by the Committee and the 
comments/clarifications of the Ministry are reproduced in the succeeding paragraphs.

INTRODUCTION 
1. I, the Chairman of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having been 
authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf, this Two Hundred and Twenty 
Eighth Report of the Committee.  
2.  The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya  Sabha has been constituted under 
Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of B usiness in the Council of States.  The 
mandate of the Committee is to scrutinize and repor t to the Council whether the powers to 
make rules, regulations, bye-laws, schemes or other  statutory instruments conferred by the 
Constitution or delegated by Parliament have been p roperly exercised within such 
conferment or delegation as the case may be.   
3. The Committee's concern is centered mainly aroun d the serious implications of 
delayed framing of rules/regulations/orders, etc de spite the Committee’s several 
recommendations on the issue and repeated observati ons in its reports that rules/regulations 
should be framed within six months of the coming in to force of the Act.  The Committee has 
been calling the defaulting Ministries/ Departments  to know the reason for the delay, the 
problems faced by them in framing the rules/regulat ions, etc and to find solutions to the 
problems.  
4. In this Report, the issue of delay in framing of  rules/regulations under Acts 
administered by various Ministries/Departments of t he Government of India  and the issue of 
legality of Master Circulars issued by the Reserve Bank of India under the Banking 
Regulation Act, 1949 have been covered.  The Report  contains general as well as specific 
observations/recommendations of the Committee on the subject. 
 
5. The   Committee considered and adopted the draft  Report in its meeting held on the 
9
th  August 2016.

      INTRODUCTION 
 
1. BACKGROUND 
 
 Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in 
the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) provides that there shall be a 
Committee on Subordinate Legislation to scrutinize and report to the 
Council whether the powers to make rules, regulations, bye-laws, 
schemes or other statutory instruments conferred by the Constitution 
or delegated by Parliament have been properly exercised within such 
conferment or delegation, as the case may be.  
1.2. Mandate  
 Legislations passed by the Parliament and subsequently 
enacted after being assented to by the President of India, are 
implemented by the Executive i.e., various Ministries/Departments of 
Government of India. It is a well recognized principle that the laws 
enacted by Parliament cannot be exhaustive enough to visualize each 
and every situation that may arise during the course of its 

implementation and to make provisions for it in the Act in 
anticipation. The Central Acts, therefore, if necessary,  contain a 
provision authorizing the Government to frame detailed 
rules/regulations, etc. to enable it to implement the provisions of the

REPORT  
 THE CONSUMER PROTECTION (E-COMMERCE) RULES, 2020  
  
I. BACKGROUND 
 
“A customer is the most important visitor on our premises. He is not dependent on us. We are 
dependent on him. He is not an interruption in our work – he is the purpose of it. We are not 
doing him a favor by serving him. He is doing us a favor by giving us the opportunity to serve 
him.” 
–Mahatma Gandhi   
 The Information Technology revolution at the begin ning of the new century brought about a 
transformation in the way in which Commerce and Bus iness are conducted throughout the 
world. The new terminologies like ‘dot com’ and ‘e’-version companies over-shadowed the old 
brick-and-mortar business industries. Technology an d Business are becoming inextricably 
interwoven and this has fostered the growth of e-Co mmerce Industry. e-Commerce means 
application of electronics in Commerce. The influx of the Internet and World Wide Web has 
made it possible to communicate and transact over cyberspace and made the whole world into a 
'Global village'. This transformation has also brought a number of challenges like cyber crimes, 
quality issues, and payment related frauds and a pressing need for its regulation has emerged as 
a prime concern for the authorities. At the pace wi th which the e-Commerce industries are 
growing, regulation of this sector along with educa ting consumers about their rights has 
become vital for healthy growth of e Commerce industries. 
2. The emergence of global supply chains, rise in i nternational trade and the rapid development 
of e-Commerce have led to new delivery systems for goods and services and have provided

Introduction 
India has, in  the recent past, witnessed a series of financial frauds in the 
form of ponzi schemes, chit fund scams and other such unregulated deposit 
schemes which have robbed the people of their hard -earned savings. 
Companies/institutions/individuals running such sch emes exploit the existing 
regulatory gaps and lack of strict administrative and legislative measures to 
dupe a large number of people. The most affected victims of these schemes 
have been the poor, gullible and financially illiterate people who fall prey t o 
such schemes easily. In 2016, the then Finance Minister had proposed to bring 
in a comprehensive Central legislation during his Union Budget speech to deal 
with the menace of such schemes. Subsequently, 'the Banning of Unregulated 
Deposit Scheme Ordinanc e, 2019’ was promulgated on 21st February, 2019 in 
order to deter the operators from running such illicit deposit schemes and to ban 
them. The Ordinance was then replaced by ‘the Banning of Unregulated Deposit 
Schemes Act, 2019’  (Annexure I), which received the assent of the President 
on the 31st July, 2019. The Act aims to protect investors/innocent people from 
fraudulent investment schemes. The Act covers existing gaps in legislation that 
had been exploited by various parties to siphon off large amount of money from 
small and innocent investors. Section 37 of the Act provides for Rules to be 
made by the Central Government for carrying out the provisions of the Act. In 
exercise of the powers conferred by Section 37 of the Act, the Central 
Government notifie d the  Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Rules, 
2020, (Annexure I I) which were published in the Gazette of India on the 
12th February, 2020.

CHAPTER I 
1.         BACKGROUND 
      Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States (Rajya Sabha) provides that there shall be a Committee on 
Subordinate Legislation to scrutinize and report to the Council whether the 
powers to make rules, regulations, bye -laws, sc hemes or other statutory 
instruments conferred by the Constitution or delegated by Parliament have 
been properly exercised within such conferment or delegation, as the case 
may be. 
1.2.      Mandate  
            Legislations passed by the Parliament and subsequently enacted 
after being assented to by the President of India, are implemented by the 
Executive i.e., various Ministries/Departments of Government of India. It is 
a well recognized principle th at the laws enacted by Parliament cannot be 
exhaustive enough to visualize each and every situation that may arise 
during the course of their implementation and to make provisions for it in 
the Act in anticipation. The Central Acts, therefore, if necessary ,  contain a 
provision authorizing the Government to frame detailed rules/regulations, 
etc. to enable it to implement the provisions of the Act. These 
rules/regulations framed in exercise of the powers conferred by an Act of 
Parliament are termed as Subordinate Legislation. 
Rule 209 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States lays down that after each rule, regulation, bye -law, 
scheme or other statutory instrument framed in pursuance of the 
Constitution/Act or the legislative functions delegated by the Parliament to

INTRODUCTION 
 
1.  I, the Chairman of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having 
been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this Two 
Hundred and Fifty Second Report of the Committee. 
2. The Committee examined the matters that came up while scruti nizing the 
Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 and issue relating to 
them along with the comments received from the Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change. The Ministry has notified Wetlands (Conservation 
and Management Rules, 20 17 under the provisions of the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986 as regulatory framework for conservation and 
management of wetlands in India.  
3. The above Rules were framed under Sub -section (1) and clause (v) of 
Sub-section (2) and Sub-section (3) of Section 3 of the Environment Protection 
Act, 1986. The Wetlands Conservation and Management is an important and 
crucial area. These rules fortify the legal framework for environmental concerns 
and strengthen the institutional framework through State/UT Wetland 
Authorities and the National Wetland Committee.  
4. The Committee’s observations/recomm endations are contained in the 
Report.

held on 5th October, 2023.

INTRODUCTION 
1.  I, the Chairman of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having been 
authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this Two Hundred and 
Fifty Third Report of the Committee. 
2. The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha is constituted under 
Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States. 
The mandate of the Committee is to scrutinize  and report to Rajya Sabha  whether the 
powers to make  Rules, Regulations, Bye -laws, Schemes and other statutory 
instruments conferred by the Constitution or delegated by Parliament have been 
properly exercised within such conferment or delegation as the case may be. 
3. The Rules/Regulations/Orders etc. are required to be framed within six months 
of the coming into force of the particular Act.  However, the Committee noticed that 
despite the time limit prescribed for completion of framing of subordinate legislation 
and the several ob servations and recommendations of the Committee on the matter, 
various Acts are still pending since many years in various Ministries.   
4. The Committee's apprehension is also focused around the serious implications 
of delay in making of Rules and Regulati ons. Therefore, the Ministries under whom 
Acts are pending for a considerable time were identified and heard in two spells on 
29th May and 30 th June, 2023 in the meetings held with the Ministries to know the 
reasons for delay and the problems faced by the Ministries in framing the 
rules/regulations, etc. This report is prepared on the basis of these deliberations and its 
observations/recommendations are contained in the Report.  
5. The Committee considered and adopted the draft Report in its meeting held on  
5th October, 2023.

I. Introduction and Background
1.1 The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
Bill, 2021 was introduced in Lok Sabha on July 30, 2021. This Bill provided for the constitution of a
Commission for better co-ordination, research, identification, and resolution of problems related to air
quality in the National Capital Region (NCR) and adjoining areas. Adjoining areas were defined as areas
in Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh, adjoining the National Capital Territory of Delhi and
NCR, where any source of pollution may cause adverse impact on air quality in the NCR. This Bill also
sought to dissolve the Environment Pollution Prevention and Control Authority established in the NCR in
1998. An Ordinance establishing a similar Commission was promulgated in October 2020 which lapsed
in March 2021 and was repromulgated in April 2021. This Bill repealed the 2021 Ordinance.
1.2 The Statement of Object and Reasons, with the Bill, succinctly stated that the Bill aimed to
establish a Commission for Air Quality Management in the National Capital Region (NCR) and its
adjoining areas to address the ongoing air pollution crisis while noting that despite efforts by Committees,

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairperson of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do
hereby present this Hundred and Twenty Fifth Report of the Committee.
2. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on 20.12.99.
1.3 The matters examined by the Committee arise out of the scrutiny of various Rules/Regulations and the issues, related therewith, alongwith the
Government’s comments received thereon. The observations and recommendations which, in the opinion of the Committee, should be brought to
the notice of the House, are contained in the succeeding paragraphs of the Report.

The Coir Board (Classification, Control and Appeal)
Bye Laws, 1969.
The Coir Board (Classification, Control and appeal) Bye Laws, 1969 were examined and some points were referred to the Ministry of Industry for
their comments/clarifications on January 5, 1999. 
  
 
2. The points referred and the Ministry’s Comments/clarifications received thereon are enclosed (Annexure-I).
3. The Committee had discussions on the subject with the representatives of the Coir Board and the Ministry of Industry on January 11, 1999 during
its visit to Cochin. Relevant extracts from the study note on the Committee’s visit to Cochin and Thiruvananthapuram is enclosed (Annexure-II)
which contain Committee observations on the various points in the light of the views that emerged during the course of discussion.
4. The Committee considered the above mentioned subject at its meeting held on April 1, 1999. The Committee notes with satisfaction that

REPLY TO POINTS REAISED IN THE QUESTIONNAIRE ON COIR BOARD SERVICES (CLASSIFICATION, CONTROL &
APPEAL) BYE LAWS, 1969.
1. Point referred- Whether the bye-laws have been laid on the tale of each House of Parliament. If so the details in this regard.
Reply to Point No. 1:-
As per Section 27 (4) of the Coir Industry Act, 1953 (45 of 1953), every Bye-law made under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is
made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session, for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or
more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive session aforesaid.
The Section 27 (4) was inserted in the Coir Industry Act based on the Delegated Legislation’s Provisions (Amendment) Act, 1986. Before 1986, it
was required only to notify the Bye-law made/amended in the official Gazette by the Central Government in terms of Section 27 (2) and (3) of the
Coir Industry Act, However, since 1986, every Bye-law made under the Act will have to be laid before each H

As per Section 27 (4) of the Coir Industry Act, 1953 (45 of 1953), every Bye-law made under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is

more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive session aforesaid.

The Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust Employees (Pay and Allowances) Regulations, 1997 were laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 27th July, 1998 and

Question No. 2
Regulation 2(4) "Compensatory Allowance" means an allowance included in the Schedule or approved for inclusion in the Schedule or granted
under these or any other regulations to meet personal expenditure necessitated by the special circumstances in which duty is performed. It includes a
travelling allowance.
What is the justification for including travelling allowance within the meaning of the term "compensatory allowance" when the same has been
defined separately in regulation 2(28).
 
Comments-
The definition as contained in Regulation 2(4) of the JNP Employees (Pay & Allowances) Regulation, 1997 has been borrowed from the definition
of compensatory allowance as contained in the 9(5). This definition of compensatory allowance as contained in the Fundamental Rules specifically
states that it includes travelling allowance. In Regulation 2(28) of the JNP Regulations, travelling allowance has been separately defined as an
allowance granted to the employee to cover the expenditure which he incurs on travelling in the course of his employment and it includes allowance
granted for maintenance of any mode of conveyance. It may be seen that there is no duplication between Regulation 2(28) and Regulation 2(4)
which states that travelling allowance can also be treated as compensatory allowance.

.

1.3     The notifications containing Rules/Regulations, etc. laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha during its 191st session have been perused by the
Committee in the light of the provisions of the Act under which they have been framed and also with a view to see whether they have been laid
timely and properly. The recommendations of the  Committee in this behalf are contained in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
 
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                                                              DIPANKAR   MUKHERJEE
