Health, Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy and Department of Family 
Welfare. 
            The Department of Health deals with medical and public health matters including drugs control 
and prevention of food adulteration.  It is headed by a Secretary to the Government of India who is 
supported by two Additional Secretaries. The Department has an attached office i.e. Directorate General 
of Health Services. The DGHS renders technical advice on all medical and public health matters and is 
involved in the implementation of various health schemes.  
            The Central Government has the sole executive responsibility in respect of subjects included in 
the Union List such as port quarantine including hospitals connected therewith. In regard to items 
included in the State List, such as Public Health, Hospitals and Dispensaries, the Central Govt's direct 
responsibility is restricted to UTs without legislature and providing  enabling framework for 
development of infrastructures in respect of matter falling under the Concurrent List. 
            The Central Govt.  evolves broad policies and plans through the Central Council of Health, set

REPORT 
I           INTRODUCTION 
            The Census of 2001 had indicated the population of India as 1027 million with 531 million 
males and 496 million females.    In the decade 1991-2001, nearly 181 million persons were added to the 
population of India.   Population increased at an annual exponential growth rate of 1.93 percent in the 
decade.  As per the latest Sample Registration System (SRS) estimates, the annual growth rate of 
population is 1.74% (1999).    
The eight States of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Uttaranchal, 
Chhatisgarh and Orissa, which currently constitute nearly 44% of the total population of India, are 
projected to comprise 48% of the total population in 2016.   In other words, these States alone will 
contribute an anticipated 55% increase during the period 1996-2016.    Demographic outcome in these 
States will determine the timing and size of population at which India achieves population stabilisation. 
The three most significant factors that can curtail the growth of population are increase in the use of 
contraceptives, improvement in the mother’s health and survival of children.  All the programmes of the 
Department of Family Welfare are accordingly planned and being implemented for pursuing a 
combination of these three issues.  
            During the Tenth Five-Year Plan the main thrust of family welfare programme would be: 
To assess the needs for Reproductive and Child Health (RCH); 
To provide need based, client centered and demand driven RCH care; 
To strengthen the infrastructure for service delivery and bridging the gap in essential infrastructure and 
manpower; 
Providing additional assistance to poorly performing districts and ensuring uninterrupted supply of 
drugs and equipments

organized a large number of programmes in the field of youth developments and sports and physical education.   The
Programmes undertaken by the Department are mainly Sports and Games, Physical Education and Youth Programmes.

the youth as also involving them in various nation building activities.  To achieve these objectives, Ministry of Youth
Affairs and Sports has undertaken various youth welfare programmes which range from personality development to
vocational training, to promotion of adventure and entrepreneurial development.  Most of these programmes are
implemented by State Governments, autonomous organizations of the Ministry and non-governmental organizations. 
Financial assistance is provided to all the implementing agencies by this Ministry as per the stipulated norms.  The
major schemes for youth development are National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, National
Integration Programmes, Youth Hostels and National Service Volunteers Scheme, etc. and the same are financed by the
Ministry.

centre-stage in our development planning since independence. However, it was in 1980s that women were recognised as
a separate target group and given their rightful place in developmental planning by including a separate chapter viz.,
‘Women and Development’ in the Sixth Plan Document (1980-85). This marked the breakaway from a welfare
approach to women’s problems in the earlier years. Since then, all efforts of the government have been directed towards
bringing women into the mainstream of the national development process by raising their overall status -social,
economic, political and legal - at par with that of men. The Government realised that real development cannot take roots

from 13 to 35 years and recognizes four thrust areas i.e.  (i)  youth empowerment (ii) gender justice, (iii) inter-
sectoral approach and (iv) information and research network. The policy identifies eight key  aspects like
education, health, environment, sports and recreation, art and culture, training and employment of youth. It also seeks
to accord priority to the groups of youth-rural and tribal youth, out of school youth, adolescents particularly female,
youth with disability and those under difficult circumstances.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development, having
been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this Hundred-Fifty Fourth Report on the ‘Functioning of
Navodaya Vidyalayas’.
2.         The Navodaya  Vidyalayas were set up by the Government primarily with the view to providing quality education upto
the secondary level to the children predominantly from the rural areas at an affordable cost.  These Vidyalayas, after several years
of their existence, have no doubt, shown good results but their functioning leaves a lot to be desired. Concerns have been
expressed on different aspects of their working by all concerned ¾ students, teachers, parents, educationists and the general
public as well.  The Committee also had invariably been emphasising the need for taking remedial measures for addressing those
concerns, but with no signs of visible improvement. 
3.         The Committee decided to make an indepth study of this unique and premier school system covering all aspects of its
functioning with a view to identifying the problem areas and suggesting measures for tackling them.
4.         The Committee visited several Navodaya Vidyalayas in different parts of the country and held discussions with the
teaching/non-teaching staff, students, parents, State Government authorities and also the general public.
5.         The Committee sought written replies on detailed questionnaire prepared on the basis of various documents/papers
furnished by the Department of Secondary and Higher Education and also on issues/problem areas highlighted during its on-the-
spot visits to some of  the Vidyalayas and deliberations held there.  The Committee also held extensive discussions with the
Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education and Commissioner, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and other concerned
officials on a number of occasions.

In this process various initiatives, policies, programmes, schemes and enabling measures have been evolved for the benefit of these groups covering a wide range of areas from gender equality, women and child related legislation to their social and economic rehabilitation. The schemes/programmes of the Ministry are implemented mainly with the support of State Governments, other
Government agencies and non-governmental organizations.

PREFACE
 
          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee on its behalf, do hereby present this Hundred Eighty-third
Report of the Committee on Major Issues Concerning Kendriya Vidyalayas.
 
2.         The Committee after having done an extensive study of the Functioning of Kendriya Vidyalayas had presented
the Hundred sixty-second Report to Parliament on 28 th April, 2005.  Thereafter, the Committee also considered the
Action-Taken Notes on the Report received from the Department of Secondary and Higher Education. While doing so,
the Committee found that some important issues raised by the Committee either were not explained convincingly or
further clarification were required on those. It was, therefore, decided to present another report highlighting those major
issue on which the Committee wishes to make further emphasis and obtain Government’s response.
 
3.         The Committee held extensive discussion with the representatives of the Department and Kendriya Vidyalaya
Sangathan on 3
rd and 13th January, 2006.  The Committee also heard the representative of CPWD on 6 th January, 2006
to get a correct assessment about the construction of KV buildings.
 
4.         The Draft report prepared on the basis of the feedback received from the Department and the discussions held
with the concerned authorities was considered and adopted by the Committee on the 27
th September, 2006.

1.1       The system of education in India has broadly been divided into three categories: elementary education, secondary
education and higher education. Prior to 12
th July, 2006, these three categories were being looked after by two Departments under
the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India. The Department of School Education & Literacy was in-
charge of elementary education and the Department of Secondary & Higher Education looked after the secondary and higher
education components. However, following amendments to Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the
Departments have been renamed as ‘Department of School Education & Literacy’ and ‘Department of Higher Education’. Thus,
the component of secondary education has now been transferred (from the erstwhile Department of Secondary & Higher
Education) to the present Department of School Education & Literacy. This Report deals with the Demands for Grants, 2007-08,
pertaining to the Department of Higher Education. Broadly, the functions of the Department of Higher Education are to evolve
educational policy in all its aspects and to coordinate and determine standards in higher education including research.  The
Department is also entrusted with the responsibility to expand and develop technical education; to improve quality of textbooks;
to administer scholarships and other schemes; to foster and encourage studies and research in Sanskrit and other classical
languages and to coordinate its functions with the programmes of assistance and other activities of UNESCO.

upgraded to the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports.  On 17th May, 2000 it became a full fledged Ministry.

of Youth and Adolescents, and the functions of the Central Government with regard to Sports and Physical Education.

schemes are proposed to be re-oriented as a part of an integrated framework comprising three key thrust areas viz.,
Personality Development, Preparation for Work Participation/Employability, and Empowerment.

REPORT
 
I        INTRODUCTION
 
1.1     The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports (MoYAS) is entrusted with the responsibilities relating to
the development of Youth and Adolescents, as also the promotion of Sports and Physical Education in
the country. There is a close relationship between these two aspects as the Sports and Physical
Development are vital ingredients of an inclusive Development of the youth, apart from its other aspects
pertaining to competitive Sports.
 
1.2
             Accordingly, the MoYA&S is implementing a large number of schemes for the development of
youth and adolescents development as well as promotion of sports in the country.  As regards those
relating to youth, the schemes are proposed to be re-oriented as a part of an integrated framework
comprising three key thrust areas viz., Personality Development, Preparation for Work
Participation/Employability, and Empowerment.
 
1.3     The Committee appreciates the reorientation of the fragmented Schemes into an integrated
framework with a multi-pronged approach towards youth empowerment and their participation
in the planning of their development.

a report (193rd Report) on the implementation of these three schemes in North-Eastern States and Jammu

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee present this 
Two Hundred- Eighteenth Report of the Committee on ‘The National Commission for 
Minority Educational Institutions (Amendment) Bill, 2009*. 
 
2. In pursuance of Rule 270 relating to the Department-re lated Parliamentary 
Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok 
Sabha referred** ‘The National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions 
(Amendment) Bill, 2009 as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 7
th August, 2009 and 
pending therein, to the Committee on the 14 th September, 2009 for examination and 
report within three months. 
 
3. The Committee considered the Bill in four sittings held on the 24 th September, 
8th October, 20th October and 30th October, 2009.  The Committee heard the views of the 
representatives of the Department of Higher Education (Ministry of Human Resource 
Development) and Chairman, National Commission for Minority Educational 
Institutions.  The Committee in its sitting held on the 30 th October, 2009 took up 
‘clause-by-clause consideration’ of the Bill 
 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft Report on the 12 th November, 
2009.  
 
5. The Committee has relied on the following in finalizing the Report: 
 
(i) Background Note on the Bill; 
(ii) Clause –by-Clause Note on the Bill; 
(iii) Oral evidence on the Bill; and 
(iv) Replies on the questionnaire received from the Department; 
 
6. On behalf of the Committee, I would like to thank the officials of the 
Department of Higher Education for providing necessary inputs and clarifications on the 
provisions of the bill. 
 
7. For facility of reference, observations and recommendations of the Committee 
have been provided in bold letters in the body of the Report.

Two Hundred Sixty Second Report of the Committee on the ‘Functioning of National Sports

Development constituted a Sub-Committee on the ‘Functioning of National Sports Federations’ for
detailed examination of the subject under the convenorship of Shri Avinash Rai Khanna, MP, Rajya
Sabha. The Sub-Committee had a detailed examination of the subject with special focus on the
development and promotion of the sports disciplines, holding of national/international sports events
by National Sports Federations, training/coaching of sportspersons, problem areas in the functioning
of the federations, coordination with the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports and other bodies and
suggestions for improvement of the same.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human
Resource Development, having been authorized by the Committee, present this Two Hundred and
Sixty Fourth Report of the Committee on the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children)
Bill, 2014.
*
2. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Bill, 2014 was introduced in the Lok
Sabha on the 12
th August, 2014. In pursuance of Rule 270 relating to the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred ** the Bill to the Committee
on 19 th September, 2014 for examination and report.
3. The Bill seeks to consolidate and amend the law relating to children alleged and found to
be in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection by catering to their basic
needs through proper care, protection, development, treatment, social re-integration, by adopting
a child-friendly approach in the adjudication and disposal of matters in the best interest of
children and for their rehabilitation through processes provided, and institutions and bodies
established. The Committee issued a Press Release on 29
th September, 2014 for eliciting public
opinion on the Bill. The Committee received a total number of 38 memoranda in response to the
Press Release. The Committee held extensive deliberations on the Bill with the stakeholders which

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorized by the Committee, present this Two Hundred and Ninety Ninth Report
of the Committee on the National Sports University Bill, 2017. (Annexure I)
2. The National Sports University Bill, 2017 (NSU) was introduced in Lok Sabha on the 10th August,
2017 and referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha on the 24th
August, 2017 for examination and report.
3. The National Sports University Bill, 2017 (NSU) seeks to establish and incorporate a National Sports
University in the State of Manipur, specialized University first of its kind, to promote sports education in the
areas of sports sciences, sports technology, sports management and sports coaching besides functioning as
the national training centre for select sports disciplines by adopting best international practices and for
matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
4. The Committee also issued a Press Communiqué on 31st October, 2017 in print and electronic media
to seek the views of the people on the Bill. The Committee held extensive deliberations on the Bill with the
stakeholders which included Secretary, Department of Sports, Director, Lakshmibai Institute for Physical
Education, Dean, Guru Nanak Dev University, Head, Department of Physical Education and Sciences, Delhi
University and Director, Sports Injury Centre, Safdarjung Hospital in its meeting held on 16th October, and
13th December, 2017 and 4th January, 2018.  The Committee also interacted with the State Government of
Manipur on the Bill. The Committee also took note of the written submissions of the stakeholders. Views of
the stakeholders and comments of the Department were taken note of while formulating the observations
and recommendations of the Committee.

PREFACE 
I, the Chairman of the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports , having been authorised by the Committee 
to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Thirty First 
Report of the Committee on “Reforms in Content and Design of School Text books”.   
 
2.  In the Indian education system school textbooks prepared by NCERT and its manner of 
presentation of content, designing and coverage of the subject is the primary tool that guides 
the education of school students across the cou ntry. In this backdrop, no ting their role in 
shaping our future generations and their learning, the Committee had decided to take up the 
subject for examination and seek inputs from all stakeholders for their improvement.  In this 
regard, the Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Department of School Education & 
Literacy alongwith Director, NCERT and Chairman, CBSE in the meeting held on 13 th 
January, 2021 on the subject. The Committee also heard the views of Prof. J.S. Rajput, 
Former Director, NCERT and representatives of Bhartiya Shikshan Mandal on the same 
day. The Committee also held discussions with representatives of Janana Probodhini, 
Pratham Education Foundation, Central Square Foundation and Vidya  Bharathi on 21 st  
January, 2021 and of Public Policy Research Centre on 21 st June, 2021. The  Committee 
also  heard the  views of  Samvit Research Foundation and Professor Nachiketa Tiwari, IIT  
Kanpur alongwith  Shri  Hukmdev Narayan  Yadav, Ex -MP, Lok Sabha in its meeting  held 
on 23 rd  July, 2021.

PREFACE 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Thirty Fifth 
Report of the Committee on the subject "Reforms in the Education of Performing and Fine 
Arts".  
2. Arts and Culture are the two important ingredients that shape the characteristics of 
any civilisation. India is not just a country, it is a civilisation with a history of many 
millennia. As rightly described by Pt Deendayal Upadhyay our civilisational journey has 
always been through continuity with change as it always has been ‘From the past, through the 
present and to the future’!  In this endless journey, Arts and Culture play the role of a vehicle. 
Mahatma Gandhi had once observed that “All true art must help the soul to realize its inner 
self”. Combining the ethos these thoughts espouse and the way our educational system is 
undergoing the change envisaged by the National Education Policy 2020 which affirms that 
"The curriculum must include basic arts, crafts, humanities, games, sports and fitness, 
languages, literature, culture, and values, in addition to science and mathematics, to develop 
all aspects and capabilities of learners; and make education more well-rounded, useful, and 
fulfilling to the learner”, the Committee  had taken up this subject for examination and to 
make its observations/ recommendations  which can help further the cause of adding more 
value to education of Performing and Fine arts in our country through a slew of reforms.  
3. During the course of its deliberations on the subject, the Committee interacted with 
representatives of the Ministry of Culture, Department of School Education & Literacy and 
Department of Higher Education of the Ministry of Education and the representatives of 
Centre for Culture Resources and Training, Lalit Kala Akademi, Sangeet Natak Akademi,

PREFACE 
I, the Chairman of the Department -Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Fifty Sixth Report of 
the Committee on "Implementation of the National Education Policy, 2020 in Higher Education". 
 
2. The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, 
Children, Youth and Sports, has been examining the implementation National Education Policy 
(NEP) 2020  and the current Report is on aspects of the NEP and the vision it lays out vis-a- vis its 
rollout during the years since its launch in the Higher Education Sector. The Committee wishes to 
place on record its gratitude to the representatives of the Department of Higher Education , 
Ministry of Education for furnishing necessary information/documents and rendering valuable 
assistance to the Committee in its deliberations.  The Committee also exp resses its gratitude to 
two of the country’s esteemed Institutions -Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai (TISS) and 
Institute of Rural Management, Anand (IRMA) for presenting their views to the Committee in its 
deliberations.  
 
3. The Committee would a lso like to appreciate the cooperation and inputs given by 
representatives of Department of Financial services, Ministry of Finance; various Public Sector 
Banks; State Governments/ UTs during its study visits.  
 
4. For the facility of reference and convenience, the recommendations of the Committee have 
been presented in bold letters in the body of the Report. 
 
5. The Committee considered the draft Report and adopted the sam e in its meeting held on 
the 20th September, 2023.  
 
 
 
NEW DELHI 
20th Sept

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, 
Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to present the 
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Seventy-Seventh Report of the 
Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 101) of the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development for the year 2026–27. 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India projected under various 
Demands for Grants for the ensuing financial year is required to be voted by Parliament. 
Consequently, the Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand referred to the 
concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee for detailed scrutiny under Rule 
270 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). 
While scrutinising the Demands for Grants, the Committee has made an appraisal of the 
performance, programmes, schemes and policies of the Ministry of Women and Child Development 
vis-à-vis the expenditure incurred out of the Consolidated Fund of India during the current financial 
year. 
 
3. In this Report, a scrutiny of the Budget allocations of the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development as sought under Demand No. 101 for the Financial Year 2026-27 has been made by

1.1. Education is the key to all processes of development, especially human development. Having regard to
the size of the population, diversity and economic frailties prevailing in the country, the challenges in the
path of providing Education for All are too many and enormous. Education being in the Concurrent List,
its meaningful development implies an effective partnership between the Union Govt. and the states. While
the role and responsibility of states to provide education continues to remain essentially unchanged, the
Union Department of Education has assumed a larger responsibility to reinforce the national and integrated
character of education, to look after the international aspects of Education and in general, to promote
excellence in all sectors of education throughout the country.

the Ninth Plan indicates that "apart from carrying out the directions given by the National Policy on
Education, 1986 and NPA, 1992, making the nation fully literate by the year 2005 will be a committed
goal. Priorities, therefore, include universalisation of elementary education, raising the quality of education
at all levels, upliftment of the educational status of disadvantaged groups like SCs/STs/girls/disabled,
equality and removal of regional imbalances, vocationalisation of education and setting up of centres of
excellence".

I INTRODUCTION  
1.1 The Department of Culture plays a vital role in the promotion and dissemination of art and 
culture. The aim of the Department is to develop ways and means for instilling basic values and 
perceptions in the minds of the people, particularly the young. The Department also undertakes 
the prgoramme of preservation, encouragement and dissemination of various manifestations of 
creative activity, both past and present. The Department is engaged in excavation, conservation 
and promotion of ancient monuments and historic sites; administration of libraries, museums and 
institutions of anthropology; collection, preservation and ethnology of national character; catering 
to institutions and organisations in the areas of Buddhist and Tibetan Studies; promoting literary, 
visual and performing arts; observing centenaries and anniversaries of important personalities 
and entering into cultural agreements with foreign countries. The Department carries out its 
various programmes through two attached offices, six subordinate offices and 26 autonomous 
organisations.  
1.2 During the Ninth Five Year Plan period, the Department proposes to focus on a 
comprehensive plan for preservation of the archeological heritage and development of the 
monumental complexes in the country. Efforts would also be directed towards the preservation of 
archival heritage and the promotion of classical, folk and tribal art and crafts and oral traditions 
which are threatened with extinction.

INTRODUCTION
1.1. India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population. According to the
1998 United Nations Fund Population Activities (UNFPA) - estimates, population of India is increasing at the rate of
1.55 crores per year. And on current trends, in 2050 India will become the most populous country with population of
152 crores. Such an alarming scenario has big implications for the problem of unemployment and state of environment
in the country.
1.2. The current high population growth rate is mainly due to the three major factors as enumerated below:
1. large size of the population in the reproductive age group;
2. higher fertility due to unmet need for contraception; and
3. high wanted fertility due to prevailing high Infant Mortality (IMR).
The All India average annual exponential growth rate during the last decade has been of the order of 2.14% which is
marginally lower than 2.22% during the previous decade. As per the latest 1996 SRS estimates, it is 1.85%, but it is
still very high when compared with the developed nations of the world.
1.3. The main objective of the Family Welfare Programme since beginning has been to stabilise population of the
country at a level consistent with the requirements of national development. The objective is pursued by addressing
contraception issues, maternal health issues, child survival issues and by encouraging citizens through IEC to use

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The National Health Policy  of  1983 visualised the importance of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy
and its role in the national health care system.    People of our Country have faith in the traditional systems especially
when the services provided are cheaper and available in  very  small  place  and rural areas.  Moreover, the remedies are
free from side-effects.  India has  a  large resource  of ISM&H practitioners of Homoepathy whose services need to be
fully utilised in the national health care delivery  system.    For this  purpose,  a  new  Department  of  Indian Systems of
Medicine and  Homoeopathy (ISM&H) has been set up to promote and develop the  Indian systems of Medicine
(Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy and drugless Therapies like  Yoga  and  Naturopathy). 
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
2.1. The total allocation, both Plan and Non-Plan  taken  together, provided to  the Department for the year 1998-99 was
Rs.  85.60 crores  in BE which was enhanced to 89.12 crores at RE stage.    The  Committee  has  observed  that  the 
increase at the RE stage in 1998-99 was made only in Non-Plan head i.e.  from Rs.  36.60  crores  to  40.12 crores. 
2.2. On a specific query regarding amount sought by the Department for 1999-2000, the Committee was informed that
an  amount of Rs.  106.88 crores (Rs.   63.45  crores Plan  + Rs.  43.43 crores Non-Plan) was sought and the approved
amount was Rs.  100.96 crores (Rs.  59.13 crores Plan  +  Rs.    41.83 crores  Non Plan).  Thus there is an increase of
Rs. 15.36 crores in 1999-2000 as compared to the allocation made in BE 1998-99.

AN OVERVIEW 
There are two main components of the Department i.e. Cultur~ and Arts . . A . separate 
department, called the Department of Arts, was constituted in August, 1985 with the aim 9f setting 
up the Indir a Gandhi National Centre for Arts (IGNCA)-a major centre for Arts, Humanities and 
Cultural heritage . The vast treasure of our culture is being preserved, promoted and propagated 
jointly by the Central and State Governments and Union Territ ory Administrations through out the 
country. The Archaeological survey of India is the largest and most important part of the Department 
of Culture engaged in conservation and excavation of old historical sites and about 25 per cent of the 
total budget provisions of the Department of Culture goes to this institution. Awareness generation 
and dissemination of information about our glorious past is done through exhibition of antiquities and 
artefacts preserved in museum s spread thr oug hout the country. Different Academies, National School 
of Drama, Centre for Cultural Resources and Training , Zonal Cultural Centres: Libraries , Memorials 
like Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, Kalakshetra, Madras etc., functioning under the Depart ment 
of Culture, cater to the artistic and literary needs of the people. The Anthmpological Survey of India , 
a subordinate office of the Departm ent, has been carrying out researches on cultural aspects of Indian 
population. 
2. The total outlay on culture during the Eighth Five Year Plan (as initially approved for the 
Departmen t of Culture) amounts to Rs . 727 crores (including both Central as well as State sectors).

INTRODUCTION
1.1       With the Constitutional mandate of 1950  under Article 45 Chapter IV, Directive Principles of State Policy,
which states “the State shall endeavour to provide within a period of ten years from the commencement of this
Constitution for free and compulsory education to all children until they complete the age of 14 years”  and efforts of
83
rd Amendment focussing on making Elementary Education a Fundamental Right, provision of universal elementary
education has been strongly upheld and  made a salient feature of National Policy since independence.   This resolve has
been vigorously spelt out in the National Policy on Education (NPE) 1986 and the Programme of Action (POA) 1992.   
Social justice and equity are by themselves a strong argument for providing basic education for all.   It is an established
fact that basic education improves the level of human well-being especially with regard to population control, life
expectancy, infant mortality, nutritional status of children etc.   Studies have also shown that universal basic education
significantly contributes to economic growth.

schools with 86000 teachers in 1950-51 which has increased to 1.90 lakh upper primary schools with 12.78 lakh

I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       Secondary Education marks a critical stage of education where process of transformation from childhood to
adulthood occurs.   In this phase children complete 10 years of basic education and 2 years of specialized education in
chosen fields including vocational stream.   It is the stage  where their knowledge and skills are tested for the first time
in public examinations conducted by various Boards.   It stands as a gateway to higher education for some and a stage
for entry into the world of work for others.
1.2       Higher Education, being at the apex of the educational pyramid,  has a key role to play in the education system.  
The National Policy on Education (NPE 1986)   visualizes higher education to be more dynamic and of high quality
because higher education   provides people an opportunity to reflect on the critical social, economic, cultural and
spiritual issues facing humanity.   Therefore, if the country has to make a progress, the importance of higher education
cannot be denied.

1.1       Secondary Education marks a critical stage of education where process of transformation from childhood to
adulthood occurs.   In this phase children complete 10 years of basic education and 2 years of specialized education in
chosen fields including vocational stream.   It is the stage  where their knowledge and skills are tested for the first time
in public examinations conducted by various Boards.   It stands as a gateway to higher education for some and a stage
for entry into the world of work for others.
1.2       Higher Education, being at the apex of the educational pyramid,  has a key role to play in the education system.

because higher education   provides people an opportunity to reflect on the critical social, economic, cultural and

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authoris.ed by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Eleventh Report of the Committee on the Dr. B.R. Ambedkar University Bill, 1994, alongwith 
the Bill, as amended by the Committee. · 
2. The Bill, which was introduced in.the Rajya Sabha on.the 9th May, 1994, seeks to establish 
and incorporate a teaching and residential University in the State of Uttar Pradesh and to provide for 
matters connected thereWith or incidental thereto. In pursuance of the rules relating to Department­
related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred* .the Bill, to the 
Committee for examination arid report. 
3. A Press Communique, inviting suggestions from various individuals, organisations and 
institutions interested in the subject matter of the Bill, was issued on 24th May, 1994 (Appendix-I). 
4. Twelve memoranda, containing views, opinions, comments and suggestions on the various 
provisions and aspects of the Bill, were received by the Committee. (List at Appendix-IT)'. 
5. The Committee, in its meeting held on the 8th July, 1994, decided that the memoranda received 
by it be sent to the Ministries of Human Resource DevelopmenVLaw, Justice and Company. Affairs 
for obtaining their comments for its consideration. The comments from the concerned Ministries were 
received and considered by the Committee. · 
6. The Committee considered the Bill in seven sittings (Appendix-III) and heard the oral evidence 
of 8 witnesses, including the representatives of Ministries of Human Resource Development 
· (Department of Education) and Law, Justice and Company Affairs (Department of Legal Affairs and 
Legislative Department). Besides, the Committee also heard the views of some eminent Members of 
Parliament. 
7. In its meeting held on the 18th August, 1994 the Committee considered the Draft Report 
and adopted it for presentation/laying in both the Houses. 
8. The Department of Education,. in their detailed note on the subject sub~itted to the 
Committee, explained the need for introduction of the Bill and the circumstances under which the 
University, initially proposed to be set up as a State University, is now sougnt to be set up as a Central 
University. (Appendix-N) 
9. The Secretary, Department of Education, during the course of his oral evidence before t~e 
Committee, stated that one of the unique features of this University is to gives it a distinct bias in favour 
of science and key and frontier areas qf technology, as compared to any other University. 
10. However, some Members expressed the view that the objects of the University, as contained 
in Clause 4 and Schedule 1 of the Bill, do not provide for teaching of subjects near and dear to the 
heart of Dr. B.A. Ambedkar, on whose name the University is being set up. The Committee is of the 
view that a specific provision should be included on this so as to promote the study of the ideology 
and philosophy for which Dr. Ambedkar stood and strove throughout his lif

Health, Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy and Department of Family 
Welfare. 
            The Department of Health deals with medical and public health matters including drugs control 
and prevention of food adulteration.  It is headed by a Secretary to the Government of India who is 
supported by two Additional Secretaries. The Department has an attached office i.e. Directorate General 
of Health Services. The DGHS renders technical advice on all medical and public health matters and is 
involved in the implementation of various health schemes.  
            The Central Government has the sole executive responsibility in respect of subjects included in 
the Union List such as port quarantine including hospitals connected therewith. In regard to items 
included in the State List, such as Public Health, Hospitals and Dispensaries, the Central Govt's direct 
responsibility is restricted to UTs without legislature and providing  enabling framework for 
development of infrastructures in respect of matter falling under the Concurrent List.

REPORT 
I           INTRODUCTION 
            The Census of 2001 had indicated the population of India as 1027 million with 531 million 
males and 496 million females.    In the decade 1991-2001, nearly 181 million persons were added to the 
population of India.   Population increased at an annual exponential growth rate of 1.93 percent in the 
decade.  As per the latest Sample Registration System (SRS) estimates, the annual growth rate of 
population is 1.74% (1999).    
The eight States of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Uttaranchal, 
Chhatisgarh and Orissa, which currently constitute nearly 44% of the total population of India, are 
projected to comprise 48% of the total population in 2016.   In other words, these States alone will 
contribute an anticipated 55% increase during the period 1996-2016.    Demographic outcome in these 
States will determine the timing and size of population at which India achieves population stabilisation. 
The three most significant factors that can curtail the growth of population are increase in the use of 
contraceptives, improvement in the mother’s health and survival of children.  All the programmes of the 
Department of Family Welfare are accordingly planned and being implemented for pursuing a 
combination of these three issues.  
            During the Tenth Five-Year Plan the main thrust of family welfare programme would be: 
To assess the needs for Reproductive and Child Health (RCH); 
To provide need based, client centered and demand driven RCH care; 
To strengthen the infrastructure for service delivery and bridging the gap in essential infrastructure and 
manpower; 
Providing additional assistance to poorly performing districts and ensuring uninterrupted supply of 
drugs and equipments

propagation of ISM&H, namely, Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and 
to fully utilise the potentials of these systems. 
The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM& H) is headed by a Secretary 
to the Government of India who is assisted by a Joint Secretary and four Directors/Deputy Secretaries, 4 
Advisers and several Deputy Advisors of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani &. Homoeopathy. Senior level posts

Development to give the much-needed impetus to the holistic development of women and children.

women and children and guides and coordinates the efforts of both governmental and non-governmental organizations
working in the field of women and child development.   Apart from this, the Department implements certain innovative

I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       The main responsibility of the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports is to ensure qualitative and quantitative
improvements in Youth Programmes and also on broad basing and bringing about awareness of sports and physical
fitness amongst school children and youth.  Over the years, the Ministry has taken a number of new initiatives and
organized a large number of programmes in the field of youth developments and sports and physical education.   The
Programmes undertaken by the Department are mainly Sports and Games, Physical Education and Youth Programmes.
1.2       The Ministry pursues the twin objectives of man making and nation building i.e. developing the personality of
the youth as also involving them in various nation building activities.  To achieve these objectives, Ministry of Youth
Affairs and Sports has undertaken various youth welfare programmes which range from personality development to
vocational training, to promotion of adventure and entrepreneurial development.  Most of these programmes are
implemented by State Governments, autonomous organizations of the Ministry and non-governmental organizations. 
Financial assistance is provided to all the implementing agencies by this Ministry as per the stipulated norms.  The
major schemes for youth development are National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, National
Integration Programmes, Youth Hostels and National Service Volunteers Scheme, etc. and the same are financed by the
Ministry.
1.3       The Department also finances a number of programmes which aim at promotion of sports, including creation of
sports infrastructure in different parts of the country, grants for laying of synthetic surfaces, spotting and nurturing of
talents through the schemes of Sports Authority of India, grants to National Sports Federations, National
Championships, organisation of tournaments for rural youth, women in the North-Eastern Region.

centre-stage in our development planning since independence. However, it was in 1980s that women were recognised as

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development, having
been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this Hundred-Fifty Fourth Report on the ‘Functioning of
Navodaya Vidyalayas’.
2.         The Navodaya  Vidyalayas were set up by the Government primarily with the view to providing quality education upto
the secondary level to the children predominantly from the rural areas at an affordable cost.  These Vidyalayas, after several years
of their existence, have no doubt, shown good results but their functioning leaves a lot to be desired. Concerns have been
expressed on different aspects of their working by all concerned ¾ students, teachers, parents, educationists and the general
public as well.  The Committee also had invariably been emphasising the need for taking remedial measures for addressing those
concerns, but with no signs of visible improvement. 
3.         The Committee decided to make an indepth study of this unique and premier school system covering all aspects of its
functioning with a view to identifying the problem areas and suggesting measures for tackling them.
4.         The Committee visited several Navodaya Vidyalayas in different parts of the country and held discussions with the
teaching/non-teaching staff, students, parents, State Government authorities and also the general public.
5.         The Committee sought written replies on detailed questionnaire prepared on the basis of various documents/papers
furnished by the Department of Secondary and Higher Education and also on issues/problem areas highlighted during its on-the-
spot visits to some of  the Vidyalayas and deliberations held there.  The Committee also held extensive discussions with the
Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education and Commissioner, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and other concerned
officials on a number of occasions.

REPORT
            Elementary education is the basic and critical input, which shapes the future structure as well as strength of a
society.  It ignites the young minds to its creative best and helps in turning them become capable and responsible citizens of
a nation.  Every investment in elementary education, in fact, has a cascading effect in all the areas of life. 
            Department of Elementary Education and Literacy of the Government of India formulates and implements various
programmes/schemes for providing care as well as quality education to every child of the country with special emphasis on
girls and those coming from the disadvantaged sections of society and backward areas. The Department also runs various
programmes in non-formal category to attack the problem of illiteracy through its strategies of Adult Education.
 
I           BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
1.1       The Committee notes that Plan allocation of Rs. 6000.00 crore made in BE 2004-05 for the Department of
Elementary Education and Literacy was increased to Rs. 8000.00 crore at the RE stage.    It has been further enhanced to Rs.
12531.76 crore in BE 2005-06.    The Committee is happy to learn that about 98 percent of this fund had been utilized till 30
March, 2005 under 'Elementary Education'. Under the head 'Adult Education' the performance of the Department is not

The schemes/programmes of the Ministry are implemented mainly with the support of State Governments, other

organisation of the IX Asian Games in New Delhi.   Thereafter, during the celebration of the International Youth Year
in 1985, it was converted into the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports. It became a full-fledged Ministry on the 27 th
May, 2000.

having been authorised by the Committee, present this Hundred Seventy Ninth Report of the Committee on the Sikkim
University Bill, 2006.

pending therein, to the Committee on the 4th August, 2006 for examination and report.

and adopted the draft report with amendments in clauses 5(ix), 5(xix), 21(1), 22(2), 23(2), 24(2), 25, 26, 30(1)(i), 30(1)
(k), 35(3), 39, 42 and 46 of the Act and clauses 2(1), 2(2), 9, 17, 18(2), 29(1) and 39(1) of the Statutes.

having been authorised by the Committee, present this Hundred Eighty First Report of the Committee on the Rajiv
Gandhi University Bill, 2006.

st July, 2006
and pending therein, to the Committee on the 4th August, 2006 for examination and report.

PREFACE
 
          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee on its behalf, do hereby present this Hundred Eighty-third
Report of the Committee on Major Issues Concerning Kendriya Vidyalayas.
 
2.         The Committee after having done an extensive study of the Functioning of Kendriya Vidyalayas had presented
the Hundred sixty-second Report to Parliament on 28 th April, 2005.  Thereafter, the Committee also considered the
Action-Taken Notes on the Report received from the Department of Secondary and Higher Education. While doing so,
the Committee found that some important issues raised by the Committee either were not explained convincingly or
further clarification were required on those. It was, therefore, decided to present another report highlighting those major
issue on which the Committee wishes to make further emphasis and obtain Government’s response.
 
3.         The Committee held extensive discussion with the representatives of the Department and Kendriya Vidyalaya
Sangathan on 3
rd and 13th January, 2006.  The Committee also heard the representative of CPWD on 6 th January, 2006
to get a correct assessment about the construction of KV buildings.
 
4.         The Draft report prepared on the basis of the feedback received from the Department and the discussions held
with the concerned authorities was considered and adopted by the Committee on the 27
th September, 2006.
NEW DELHI;
September27, 2006
Asvina 5,1928 (Saka)

I.            INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The system of education in India has broadly been divided into three categories: elementary education, secondary
education and higher education. Prior to 12
th July, 2006, these three categories were being looked after by two Departments under
the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India. The Department of School Education & Literacy was in-
charge of elementary education and the Department of Secondary & Higher Education looked after the secondary and higher
education components. However, following amendments to Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the
Departments have been renamed as ‘Department of School Education & Literacy’ and ‘Department of Higher Education’. Thus,
the component of secondary education has now been transferred (from the erstwhile Department of Secondary & Higher
Education) to the present Department of School Education & Literacy. This Report deals with the Demands for Grants, 2007-08,
pertaining to the Department of Higher Education. Broadly, the functions of the Department of Higher Education are to evolve
educational policy in all its aspects and to coordinate and determine standards in higher education including research.  The
Department is also entrusted with the responsibility to expand and develop technical education; to improve quality of textbooks;
to administer scholarships and other schemes; to foster and encourage studies and research in Sanskrit and other classical
languages and to coordinate its functions with the programmes of assistance and other activities of UNESCO.

of benefits should be sufficiently wide spread and equally distributed among all sections of society, especially women and
children.              As per 2001 Census of India, of the total population of 102.9 crores, there are 49.6 crores (48.3%) women.

paramount importance and sets the pace for overall development.

I           INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports, Government of India owes its origin to the Department of Sports, which
was set up in 1982 at the time of the 9
th Asian Games in New Delhi.  During the International Youth Year 1985 it was
upgraded to the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports.  On 17th May, 2000 it became a full fledged Ministry.
 
1.2       The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports (MoYAS) is entrusted with the responsibilities relating to the development
of Youth and Adolescents, and the functions of the Central Government with regard to Sports and Physical Education.
 
1.3       The MoYA&S is implementing a large number of schemes for youth and adolescents development.   These
schemes are proposed to be re-oriented as a part of an integrated framework comprising three key thrust areas viz.,
Personality Development, Preparation for Work Participation/Employability, and Empowerment.

objective of reducing the birth rate so as to stabilise the population at the level consistent 
with the Nation's !!COnomic growth and development. In spite of this, the alarming growth in 
population is one of the most pressing problems faced by the country, today . . India's 
population, which was 342 million in 1947, has touched 846.3 million according to 1991 
census and has crossed the 880 million mark by the end of 1992. 
India, presently; has about 16 per cent of the world's total population and 2.4 per cent of 
the global land area. The rapid increase in population has serious implications for the overall 
socio-economic development of the Country. Success on -the population front is vital for the 
succe ss of all developmental efforts. .

I        INTRODUCTION
 
1.1     The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports (MoYAS) is entrusted with the responsibilities relating to
the development of Youth and Adolescents, as also the promotion of Sports and Physical Education in
the country. There is a close relationship between these two aspects as the Sports and Physical
Development are vital ingredients of an inclusive Development of the youth, apart from its other aspects
pertaining to competitive Sports.
 
1.2
             Accordingly, the MoYA&S is implementing a large number of schemes for the development of
youth and adolescents development as well as promotion of sports in the country.  As regards those
relating to youth, the schemes are proposed to be re-oriented as a part of an integrated framework
comprising three key thrust areas viz., Personality Development, Preparation for Work
Participation/Employability, and Empowerment.
 
1.3     The Committee appreciates the reorientation of the fragmented Schemes into an integrated
framework with a multi-pronged approach towards youth empowerment and their participation
in the planning of their development.

Universities Bill 2008 (Annexure), as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 23 rd October, 2008 and
pending therein, to the Committee on the 14 th November, 2008 for examination and report within the
first week from the first day of next sitting of the 214 th Session of Parliament scheduled to begin on
10th December, 2008.

INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Pa rliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource 
Development, having been authorized by the Committee, present this Two Hundred and Thirteenth Report of the 
Committee on the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Bill, 2008.* 
                                                                                                                                                                                                          
2. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Educa tion Bill, 2008 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 
15th December, 2008.  In pursuance of Rule 270 rela ting to Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred the Bill on the 18 th December, 2008 to the Committee for 
examination and report within three months.  
 
3. The Committee considered the Bill in two sittings held on the 12th and 23rd January, 2009. 
 
4. On the 12 th January, 2009, the Committee heard the Secretary,  Department of School Education & Literacy 
and considered the various provisions of the Bill.  
 
5. The Committee, while drafting the report, relied on the following: 
(i) Background Note on the Bill received from the Department of School Education & Literacy; 
(ii) Note on the clauses of the Bill received fro m the Department of School Education & Literacy; 
(iii) Verbatim record of the oral evidence taken on the Bill; and 
(iv) Presentation made and clarification given by the Secretary, Department of School Education & 
Literacy.  
 
6. The Committee considered its Draft Report on the Bill and adopted the same in its meeting held on 23rd 
January, 2009. 
 
7. On behalf of the Committee, I wo uld like to thank the officials of the Department of School Education & 
Literacy for providing necessary inputs and clarifications during the consideration of the Bill.  
 
8. For facility of reference, observations and recommen dations of the Committee have been printed in bold 
letters at the end of the report.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee present this 
Two Hundred- Eighteenth Report of the Committee on ‘The National Commission for 
Minority Educational Institutions (Amendment) Bill, 2009*. 
 
2. In pursuance of Rule 270 relating to the Department-re lated Parliamentary 
Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok 
Sabha referred** ‘The National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions 
(Amendment) Bill, 2009 as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 7
th August, 2009 and 
pending therein, to the Committee on the 14 th September, 2009 for examination and 
report within three months. 
 
3. The Committee considered the Bill in four sittings held on the 24 th September, 
8th October, 20th October and 30th October, 2009.  The Committee heard the views of the 
representatives of the Department of Higher Education (Ministry of Human Resource 
Development) and Chairman, National Commission for Minority Educational 
Institutions.  The Committee in its sitting held on the 30 th October, 2009 took up 
‘clause-by-clause consideration’ of the Bill 
 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft Report on the 12 th November, 
2009.  
 
5. The Committee has relied on the following in finalizing the Report: 
 
(i) Background Note on the Bill; 
(ii) Clause –by-Clause Note on the Bill; 
(iii) Oral evidence on the Bill; and 
(iv) Replies on the questionnaire received from the Department; 
 
6. On behalf of the Committee, I would like to thank the officials of the 
Department of Higher Education for providing necessary inputs and clarifications on the 
provisions of the bill. 
 
7. For facility of reference, observations and recommendations of the Committee 
have been provided in bold letters in the body of the Report.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorized by the Committee, present this Two Hundred and Ninety Ninth Report
of the Committee on the National Sports University Bill, 2017. (Annexure I)
2. The National Sports University Bill, 2017 (NSU) was introduced in Lok Sabha on the 10th August,
2017 and referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha on the 24th
August, 2017 for examination and report.
3. The National Sports University Bill, 2017 (NSU) seeks to establish and incorporate a National Sports
University in the State of Manipur, specialized University first of its kind, to promote sports education in the
areas of sports sciences, sports technology, sports management and sports coaching besides functioning as
the national training centre for select sports disciplines by adopting best international practices and for
matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
4. The Committee also issued a Press Communiqué on 31st October, 2017 in print and electronic media
to seek the views of the people on the Bill. The Committee held extensive deliberations on the Bill with the
stakeholders which included Secretary, Department of Sports, Director, Lakshmibai Institute for Physical
Education, Dean, Guru Nanak Dev University, Head, Department of Physical Education and Sciences, Delhi
University and Director, Sports Injury Centre, Safdarjung Hospital in its meeting held on 16th October, and
13th December, 2017 and 4th January, 2018.  The Committee also interacted with the State Government of
Manipur on the Bill. The Committee also took note of the written submissions of the stakeholders. Views of
the stakeholders and comments of the Department were taken note of while formulating the observations
and recommendations of the Committee.

Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports , having been authorised by the Committee 
to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Thirty First 
Report of the Committee on “Reforms in Content and Design of School Text books”.   
 
2.  In the Indian education system school textbooks prepared by NCERT and its manner of 
presentation of content, designing and coverage of the subject is the primary tool that guides 
the education of school students across the cou ntry. In this backdrop, no ting their role in 
shaping our future generations and their learning, the Committee had decided to take up the 
subject for examination and seek inputs from all stakeholders for their improvement.  In this 
regard, the Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Department of School Education & 
Literacy alongwith Director, NCERT and Chairman, CBSE in the meeting held on 13 th 
January, 2021 on the subject. The Committee also heard the views of Prof. J.S. Rajput, 
Former Director, NCERT and representatives of Bhartiya Shikshan Mandal on the same 
day. The Committee also held discussions with representatives of Janana Probodhini, 
Pratham Education Foundation, Central Square Foundation and Vidya  Bharathi on 21 st  
January, 2021 and of Public Policy Research Centre on 21 st June, 2021. The  Committee 
also  heard the  views of  Samvit Research Foundation and Professor Nachiketa Tiwari, IIT  
Kanpur alongwith  Shri  Hukmdev Narayan  Yadav, Ex -MP, Lok Sabha in its meeting  held

PREFACE 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Thirty Fifth 
Report of the Committee on the subject "Reforms in the Education of Performing and Fine 
Arts".  
2. Arts and Culture are the two important ingredients that shape the characteristics of 
any civilisation. India is not just a country, it is a civilisation with a history of many 
millennia. As rightly described by Pt Deendayal Upadhyay our civilisational journey has 
always been through continuity with change as it always has been ‘From the past, through the 
present and to the future’!  In this endless journey, Arts and Culture play the role of a vehicle. 
Mahatma Gandhi had once observed that “All true art must help the soul to realize its inner 
self”. Combining the ethos these thoughts espouse and the way our educational system is 
undergoing the change envisaged by the National Education Policy 2020 which affirms that 
"The curriculum must include basic arts, crafts, humanities, games, sports and fitness, 
languages, literature, culture, and values, in addition to science and mathematics, to develop 
all aspects and capabilities of learners; and make education more well-rounded, useful, and 
fulfilling to the learner”, the Committee  had taken up this subject for examination and to

PREFACE 
I, the Chairman of the Department -Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Fifty Sixth Report of 
the Committee on "Implementation of the National Education Policy, 2020 in Higher Education". 
 
2. The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, 
Children, Youth and Sports, has been examining the implementation National Education Policy 
(NEP) 2020  and the current Report is on aspects of the NEP and the vision it lays out vis-a- vis its 
rollout during the years since its launch in the Higher Education Sector. The Committee wishes to 
place on record its gratitude to the representatives of the Department of Higher Education , 
Ministry of Education for furnishing necessary information/documents and rendering valuable 
assistance to the Committee in its deliberations.  The Committee also exp resses its gratitude to 
two of the country’s esteemed Institutions -Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai (TISS) and 
Institute of Rural Management, Anand (IRMA) for presenting their views to the Committee in its 
deliberations.  
 
3. The Committee would a lso like to appreciate the cooperation and inputs given by 
representatives of Department of Financial services, Ministry of Finance; various Public Sector 
Banks; State Governments/ UTs during its study visits.  
 
4. For the facility of reference and convenience, the recommendations of the Committee have 
been presented in bold letters in the body of the Report. 
 
5. The Committee considered the draft Report and adopted the sam e in its meeting held on 
the 20th September, 2023.

20th Sept

Education is an important constituent of this Ministry. During 1993-94 a budget provision of 
Rs. 2159.33 crores was made available for education in the Central Sector. This was increased to 
Rs. 2192 crores in the Revised Estimate 1993-94.

Institutes of Technology and Regional Engineering Colleges.

INTRODUCTION
1.1. Education is the key to all processes of development, especially human development. Having regard to
the size of the population, diversity and economic frailties prevailing in the country, the challenges in the
path of providing Education for All are too many and enormous. Education being in the Concurrent List,
its meaningful development implies an effective partnership between the Union Govt. and the states. While
the role and responsibility of states to provide education continues to remain essentially unchanged, the
Union Department of Education has assumed a larger responsibility to reinforce the national and integrated
character of education, to look after the international aspects of Education and in general, to promote
excellence in all sectors of education throughout the country.
The Ninth Plan treats education as the most crucial investment in human development. Approach Paper to
the Ninth Plan indicates that "apart from carrying out the directions given by the National Policy on
Education, 1986 and NPA, 1992, making the nation fully literate by the year 2005 will be a committed
goal. Priorities, therefore, include universalisation of elementary education, raising the quality of education
at all levels, upliftment of the educational status of disadvantaged groups like SCs/STs/girls/disabled,
equality and removal of regional imbalances, vocationalisation of education and setting up of centres of
excellence".

1.1. The main responsibility of the Department is to ensure qualitative and quantitative 
improvements in Youth Programmes and also on broad basing and bringing about awareness of 
sports and physical fitness amongst school children and youth. The Programmes undertaken 
by the Department are mainly Sports and Games and Youth Programmes.  
1.2. The Department finances various youth welfare programmes which ranges from 
personality development to vocational training. Most of these programmes are implemented 
by reputed institutions, non-governmental organisations as well as State Governments 
whereby financial assistance is provided by the Department as per the stipulated norms. The 
major schemes for youth development are National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra 
Sangathan, National Integration Programmes, Youth Hostels and National Service 
Volunteers Scheme,etc.

grants for laying of synthetic surfaces, spotting and nurturing of talents through 
the schemes of Sports Authority of India, grants to National Sports Federations, 
National Championships, organisation of tournaments for rural youth, women in 
the North-Eastern Region.

I INTRODUCTION  
1.1 The Department of Culture plays a vital role in the promotion and dissemination of art and 
culture. The aim of the Department is to develop ways and means for instilling basic values and 
perceptions in the minds of the people, particularly the young. The Department also undertakes 
the prgoramme of preservation, encouragement and dissemination of various manifestations of 
creative activity, both past and present. The Department is engaged in excavation, conservation 
and promotion of ancient monuments and historic sites; administration of libraries, museums and 
institutions of anthropology; collection, preservation and ethnology of national character; catering 
to institutions and organisations in the areas of Buddhist and Tibetan Studies; promoting literary, 
visual and performing arts; observing centenaries and anniversaries of important personalities 
and entering into cultural agreements with foreign countries. The Department carries out its 
various programmes through two attached offices, six subordinate offices and 26 autonomous 
organisations.  
1.2 During the Ninth Five Year Plan period, the Department proposes to focus on a 
comprehensive plan for preservation of the archeological heritage and development of the 
monumental complexes in the country. Efforts would also be directed towards the preservation of 
archival heritage and the promotion of classical, folk and tribal art and crafts and oral traditions 
which are threatened with extinction.

I. INTRODUCTION
1.1. The Department of Women and Child Development is engaged in the giving the much needed impetus
to the holistic development of women and children. The Department, as the national machinery for the
advancement of women and children, formulates plans, policies and programmes; enacts/amends
legislation; guides and coordinates the efforts of both Governmental and non-governmental organisations
working in the field of Women and Child Development. The Department also implements certain
innovative programmes for women and children covering welfare and support services, training for
employment and income generation, awareness generation and gender sensitisation. They play a
supplementary and complementary role to the other general developmental programmes in the sectors of
health, education, rural development etc. For the holistic development of the child, the Department

INTRODUCTION
1.1. India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population. According to the
1998 United Nations Fund Population Activities (UNFPA) - estimates, population of India is increasing at the rate of
1.55 crores per year. And on current trends, in 2050 India will become the most populous country with population of
152 crores. Such an alarming scenario has big implications for the problem of unemployment and state of environment
in the country.
1.2. The current high population growth rate is mainly due to the three major factors as enumerated below:
1. large size of the population in the reproductive age group;
2. higher fertility due to unmet need for contraception; and
3. high wanted fertility due to prevailing high Infant Mortality (IMR).
The All India average annual exponential growth rate during the last decade has been of the order of 2.14% which is
marginally lower than 2.22% during the previous decade. As per the latest 1996 SRS estimates, it is 1.85%, but it is
still very high when compared with the developed nations of the world.
1.3. The main objective of the Family Welfare Programme since beginning has been to stabilise population of the
country at a level consistent with the requirements of national development. The objective is pursued by addressing
contraception issues, maternal health issues, child survival issues and by encouraging citizens through IEC to use
these services.

INTRODUCTION
1.1. The National Health Policy  of  1983 visualised the importance of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy
and its role in the national health care system.    People of our Country have faith in the traditional systems especially
when the services provided are cheaper and available in  very  small  place  and rural areas.  Moreover, the remedies are
free from side-effects.  India has  a  large resource  of ISM&H practitioners of Homoepathy whose services need to be
fully utilised in the national health care delivery  system.    For this  purpose,  a  new  Department  of  Indian Systems of
Medicine and  Homoeopathy (ISM&H) has been set up to promote and develop the  Indian systems of Medicine
(Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy and drugless Therapies like  Yoga  and  Naturopathy). 
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
2.1. The total allocation, both Plan and Non-Plan  taken  together, provided to  the Department for the year 1998-99 was
Rs.  85.60 crores  in BE which was enhanced to 89.12 crores at RE stage.    The  Committee  has  observed  that  the 
increase at the RE stage in 1998-99 was made only in Non-Plan head i.e.  from Rs.  36.60  crores  to  40.12 crores. 
2.2. On a specific query regarding amount sought by the Department for 1999-2000, the Committee was informed that
an  amount of Rs.  106.88 crores (Rs.   63.45  crores Plan  + Rs.  43.43 crores Non-Plan) was sought and the approved
amount was Rs.  100.96 crores (Rs.  59.13 crores Plan  +  Rs.    41.83 crores  Non Plan).  Thus there is an increase of
Rs. 15.36 crores in 1999-2000 as compared to the allocation made in BE 1998-99.

OVERVIEW 
1. The National Health Policy (1983) has reiterated India's commitment to attain "Health for 
All (H.F .A.) by 2000 A.D.". The Eighth Plan envisages that health facilities must reach the 
entire population by the end of the Plan period. The B.F.A. paradigm, according to the 8th 
Plan, must take into account not only the high risk vulnerable groups i.e. mothers and children, 
but must also focus sharply on the underprivileged segments within the vulnerable groups. Health 
for under privileged will be the key strategy for the HFA, by the year 2000 A.D., a declaration 
to which India is a signatory. This can only be achieved by associating the pre-defined segments 
of population with not only the health planning process but also with the method for the 
, evaluation of programmes. 
2. India is facing highly complex and challenging health problems. There are health hazards 
of communicable diseases like leprosy, T.B. and malaria, besides challenges of post-transitional 
diseases like cardio-vascular and cancer. Above all these, we are also faced with horrendous 
threat of AIDS. These health problems are further aggravated by wide spread poverty, which 
leads to malnutrition, unhygienic sanitation, illiteracy and ignorance. Population growth is playing 
further havoc on the availability and quality of health services. 
3. Department of Health deals with the health administration of the country, including drugs 
control and prevention of food adulteration . 
4. The main functions of the Deparment of Health are to undertake national programmes of 
health for the prevention and eradication of communicable diseases; to promote education 
research and training in various medical disciplines; to prevent adulteration of food as well as 
drugs; to promote research and treatment on scientific lines in Indian Systems of Medicine; to 
provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people; to implement better health care 
programme for tribals, and to collaborate with WHO and other international agencies.

Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Ninety –eighth Report of the Committee on Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in the
54th Report on National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS), Bangalore.
2.         The Seventy-third Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 27 th February, 2001.  Replies of the
Government on the recommendations contained in the Report, received from the Department of Health, Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare were considered by the Committee.  Clarifications were also sought by the Committee from
the representatives of the Department.  .
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same at its meeting held on 22nd January, 2001.

authorized by the Committee to present the Report on their behalf, present 
this Fortieth Report on Action taken by the Government on the 
recommendations contained in the Thirty -Fifth Report (17th Lok Sabha) on 
Demands for Grants (2023-24) of the Ministry of Power.

March, 2023  and was laid on table of the Rajya Sabha on the same day .

contained in this Report were received on 8th June, 2023.

sitting held on 14th December, 2023.

 I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Energy, having been 
authorized by the Committee to present the Report on their behalf, present 
this Forty-First Report of the Committee on the subject ‘Bio-Energy and Waste 
to Energy – Recovery of Energy from Urban, Industrial and Agricultural 
Wastes/Residues and role of Urban Local Bodies in Energy Management ’ 
pertaining to the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy.  
2. The Committee held a briefing on the subject with representatives of the 
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, NITI Aayog and Ministry of Housing 
and Urban Affairs on 19th May, 2023. The Committee again held discussion on 
the subject with representatives of the Ministry of New and Renewable 
Energy, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and Ministry of Agriculture and 
Farmers’ Welfare on 1st June, 2023. 
3. The Committee took e vidence of representatives of the Ministry of 
Power, Central Electricity Authority , NTPC Limited, Damodar Valley 
Corporation and NLC India Limited on 15 th June, 2023. The Committee wish to 
express their thanks to all the representatives of the above mentioned 
Ministries and Organizations for appearing before the Committee and 
furnishing the desired information in connection with the issues relating to 
the subject. 
4. The Report was considered and adopted by the Committee at their 
sitting held on 14th December, 2023. 
5. The Committee place on record their appreciation for the assistance 
rendered to them by the officials of the Lok  Sabha Secretariat attached to the 
Committee.

recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in Part -
